questions.section: 1. Probability, conditional probability and Bayes' theorem
questions.prompt: A school adopts a detector that labels essays as "AI-written" or "human-written". The vendor says it is "98% accurate", meaning that it flags 98% of AI-written essays and wrongly flags 2% of human-written essays. A teacher receives a flag on one essay. (a) Compute the probability that a flagged essay really is AI-written when 5% of essays are AI-written, and again when 0.5% are, showing your counts for 10,000 essays. (b) Explain why the vendor's figure does not answer the teacher's question. (c) State what else the teacher should know before acting on a flag.

rubric.text: Distinguishes P(flagged | AI-written) = 0.98 from P(AI-written | flagged); these are different conditional probabilities and the vendor's figure is the first, not the second.
At 5% AI-written essays: 500 AI essays give 490 true flags and 9,500 human essays give 190 false flags, so 490 of 680 flags (about 72%) are correct.
At 0.5% AI-written essays: 50 AI essays give 49 true flags and 9,950 human essays give 199 false flags, so only 49 of 248 flags (about 20%) are correct.
Explains that the base rate (how common AI-written essays are) drives how trustworthy a flag is, so the same detector has very different reliability in different settings.

Names what is needed before acting: the base rate in that population, whether the false-flag rate differs across groups of writers, and corroborating evidence, treating a flag as a reason to look closer rather than as proof.

questions.section: 1. Probability, conditional probability and Bayes' theorem
questions.prompt: A forensic team searches a database of 2,000,000 people for matches to a face image from a crime scene. The system declares a match for a person who is not the source with probability 1 in 10,000, and it always matches the true source. Assume the true source is in the database. A prosecutor says: "The chance this match is a coincidence is 1 in 10,000, so there is a 99.99% chance this person is the source." Evaluate the statement with numbers, name the error, and say what additional evidence changes the conclusion.

rubric.text: Identifies the error as transposing a conditional: 1 in 10,000 is P(match | not the source), not P(not the source | match).
Computes the expected number of coincidental matches: about 2,000,000 × 1/10,000 = 200 other people matched, in addition to the true source.
Concludes that, with nothing else singling the person out, the chance a given matched person is the source is about 1 in 201, roughly 0.5%, not 99.99%.

Explains that searching a large database multiplies the opportunities for a coincidence, so the size of the search matters, and a narrower search changes the result (about 1 in 21 for a 200,000-person search).

Says independent evidence about the person (location, other identification, additional features) raises the prior odds, and that the correct combination is prior odds multiplied by the likelihood ratio.

questions.section: 1. Probability, conditional probability and Bayes' theorem
questions.prompt: Two models are evaluated on a mix of easy and hard questions. Correct answers out of questions asked: Model A scored 95 of 100 on easy questions and 300 of 900 on hard questions. Model B scored 900 of 1,000 on easy questions and 20 of 100 on hard questions. A report says "Model B is far more accurate: 83.6% against 39.5%". (a) Compute each model's accuracy on easy questions, on hard questions and overall. (b) Explain what is happening and whether the report's conclusion follows. (c) Say what comparison would be fair and what determines which breakdown to trust.

rubric.text: Computes correctly: Model A is 95% on easy, 33.3% on hard and 39.5% overall; Model B is 90% on easy, 20% on hard and 83.6% overall.
Observes that Model A is better on both easy and hard questions yet worse overall, a reversal known as Simpson's paradox.
Explains the mechanism: overall accuracy is a weighted average of group accuracies with weights set by each model's mix of questions (A mostly hard, B mostly easy).
Concludes the headline figure confounds model quality with question difficulty; a fair comparison runs both models on the same questions or standardizes both to a common mix.

Notes that the right breakdown depends on the causal story, here that difficulty is a property of the question that affects the outcome and was unevenly assigned, so the stratified comparison is the one to trust.

questions.prompt: A reliability team monitors the daily count of model failures and sets an alert at "mean plus 3 standard deviations". Their dashboard says the alert fires by chance on only about 0.13% of days (about 1 day in 740), based on the normal curve. A reviewer objects that this assumes a normal distribution. (a) Show where the 0.13% comes from. (b) Give a distribution-free statement, with its number, about how much probability can lie more than 3 standard deviations from the mean. (c) Explain why fat tails make the normal figure unreliable and what the team should do instead.

rubric.text: Shows the 0.13% as the normal upper-tail probability P(Z > 3) ≈ 0.00135, about 1 day in 740.

Gives Chebyshev's inequality: for any distribution with finite variance, at most 1/k² = 1/9 (about 11%) of the probability lies more than 3 standard deviations away in either direction, a loose worst-case guarantee compared with the normal's 0.27%.

Explains that the true figure depends on the tail shape, for example a Student t with 3 degrees of freedom rescaled to unit standard deviation puts about 1.4% beyond 3 standard deviations, around five times the normal value.

Explains that standard-deviation thresholds are calibrated only if the tail shape is right, so fat tails (and clustered failures) produce more alerts and larger extremes than the normal curve predicts.

Proposes using the data's own tail: examine histograms or quantile-quantile plots of the tail, set thresholds from empirical quantiles or extreme-value methods, use robust statistics, and track the real false-alarm rate.

questions.prompt: An autonomous agent completes a task by making 500 tool calls. Each call fails with probability 0.002 (a 99.8% per-call success rate), independently of the others, and a single failed call ruins the run. A manager calls 99.8% reliability "basically perfect". (a) Compute the expected number of failed calls per run and the probability that a run has no failure, and name the distribution and a convenient approximation. (b) What per-call failure probability would be needed for 95% of runs to succeed? (c) Explain how the independence assumption affects these numbers.

rubric.text: Identifies the number of failures as Binomial(500, 0.002) with mean 1 and variance about 1.
Computes P(no failure) = 0.998^500 ≈ 0.37, so about 63% of runs fail at least once, and notes that a Poisson distribution with mean 1 gives nearly the same value (e^−1 ≈ 0.368).
Concludes that high per-call reliability does not imply high per-run reliability, because small failure probabilities compound over many steps.
For 95% run success, solves (1 − p)^500 ≥ 0.95 to get p of about 0.0001 (roughly 1 in 10,000), about 20 times better than 0.002.

Explains that independence is an assumption: with the same per-call rate, positively correlated failures (a shared cause such as a down service) make runs with at least one failure less frequent but failures clustered, so the independent calculation can be wrong in either direction for run-level reliability.

questions.section: 3. Sampling, the central limit theorem and inference
questions.source: Statistical inference, estimation and hypothesis testing
questions.prompt: A team tests whether a new retrieval step improves a 0 to 100 answer-quality rating, with 20 rated tasks per arm and a standard deviation of about 9.8 points in each arm. The mean rating improves by 4.0 points; the standard error of the difference is 3.1 points, the two-sided p-value is 0.20, and the 95% confidence interval for the improvement is about −2.1 to +10.1 points. The team concludes "the retrieval step has no effect". (a) Explain what a p-value of 0.20 does and does not mean. (b) Critique the conclusion using the interval and the idea of statistical power. (c) State what the team should do to learn whether the step helps.

rubric.text: States that p = 0.20 means a gap at least this large would arise about 20% of the time by chance if there were no true effect; it is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true and not a measure of effect size.

Explains that failing to reject the null is not evidence of no effect (absence of evidence is not evidence of absence), because the test may simply lack the ability to detect a real effect (a Type II error).
Uses the interval: −2.1 to +10.1 includes zero but also includes sizable benefits and small harms, so the data are compatible with a large effect and the study is inconclusive.

Uses power: with 20 per arm and a standard deviation near 10 points, a true 4-point benefit would be detected only about a quarter of the time, so a non-significant result is expected even if the effect is real.

Recommends pre-specifying the smallest effect that matters and collecting more data (about 95 per arm for roughly 80% power to detect 4 points at this variability), or using an equivalence test if the claim is "no meaningful effect".

questions.section: 3. Sampling, the central limit theorem and inference
questions.source: Statistical inference, estimation and hypothesis testing
questions.prompt: A team evaluates 40 prompt variants against a baseline on the same benchmark, each with a two-sided test at significance level 0.05, and treats the 40 tests as independent. The best variant has p = 0.03 and the team announces "a statistically significant improvement". (a) If none of the variants truly differs from the baseline, how many significant results would you expect, and what is the probability of at least one? (b) Explain why the announced p-value is misleading and what per-test threshold a Bonferroni correction would use. (c) Describe two ways to handle the problem.

rubric.text: Computes the expected number of false positives, 40 × 0.05 = 2, and the probability of at least one, 1 − 0.95^40 ≈ 0.87.

Explains that the announced p-value was picked as the smallest of 40, so "a 3% chance of arising by luck" no longer applies; the chance that the smallest of 40 null p-values is 0.03 or lower is 1 − 0.97^40 ≈ 0.70.
Gives the Bonferroni threshold 0.05 / 40 = 0.00125 per test, which p = 0.03 does not meet (the adjusted p-value is 40 × 0.03, capped at 1).
Names a correction: Holm, or Benjamini–Hochberg to control the false discovery rate, or pre-registering a single primary comparison before looking.
Recommends confirming the winning variant on fresh held-out data with one pre-specified test, and reporting how many variants were tried together with effect sizes and intervals.

questions.section: 3. Sampling, the central limit theorem and inference
questions.prompt: A team runs 300 independent test prompts against a safety filter and all 300 pass. The report states "the failure rate is 0%". (a) Explain what the data do and do not show about the true failure rate. (b) Using the "rule of three" or an exact calculation, give the 95% upper bound on the failure rate. (c) How many failure-free tests would be needed to claim a failure rate below 0.1% with 95% confidence? (d) State an assumption behind these calculations.

rubric.text: Explains that zero failures in a sample does not show a true rate of zero, because a rare failure is easily missed (a true failure rate of 1% would produce no failures in 300 tests about 5% of the time, 0.99^300 ≈ 0.049).
Gives the rule of three: with n tests and no failures, the 95% upper confidence bound on the failure rate is about 3/n, so about 1% for n = 300 (exact value 1 − 0.05^(1/300) ≈ 0.99%).
Computes that an upper bound of 0.1% needs about 3 / 0.001 = 3,000 failure-free tests (the exact calculation gives about 2,995).

States an assumption: the tests are independent, representative draws from the inputs the system will actually see, so inputs not covered by the test set, near-duplicate prompts or adversarial cases are not covered by the bound.
Rewrites the claim in a defensible form: no failures in 300 tests, so the failure rate is below about 1% with 95% confidence for inputs like those tested.

questions.section: 4. Exploratory data analysis, data quality and missing data
questions.prompt: A hospital estimates 30-day readmission from follow-up calls. Of 1,000 discharged patients, the calls reach 820, so 18% of outcomes are missing. Suppose, unknown to the analyst, that 300 patients were in poor health with 50% readmitted and 700 were in good health with 10% readmitted, and that the calls reached 40% of the poor-health patients and all of the good-health patients. (a) Compute the true readmission rate and the rate the analyst sees among those reached. (b) Classify the missingness (MCAR, MAR or MNAR) in two cases: health status is recorded for every patient, and missingness depends on whether the patient was readmitted with no recorded proxy. (c) Say what the analyst should do in each case and why dropping rows or mean imputation does not fix it.

rubric.text: Computes the true rate (300 × 0.5 + 700 × 0.1) / 1,000 = 22% and the observed rate 130 / 820 ≈ 15.9%, an understatement of about 6 points.

Defines the three types: MCAR (missingness unrelated to any variable), MAR (depends only on observed variables) and MNAR (depends on the missing value itself even after accounting for observed variables).
With health status recorded, missingness depends on an observed variable (MAR), so weighting or imputing within health strata can recover the 22%.

When missingness depends on the outcome with no proxy (MNAR), the observed data cannot reveal or correct it; the analyst needs sensitivity analysis, intensive follow-up of a random sample of non-responders, or outside data.

Explains that complete-case analysis and mean imputation implicitly assume missing completely at random, so they reproduce the biased 15.9% and overstate precision; keep missingness indicators and report how much is missing.

questions.section: 4. Exploratory data analysis, data quality and missing data
questions.source: Statistical checks: test the data before you trust it
questions.prompt: A data engineer merges three source tables of loan applications into one table of 4,800,000 rows; the sources held 5,000,000 applications in total. The checks pass: no nulls, correct types, values in valid ranges, and means and standard deviations in line with last quarter. The engineer declares the dataset "clean". It later emerges that all 200,000 missing applications came from one region with 1,000,000 applications, where the default rate is 12% against 3% elsewhere. (a) Compute the overall and regional losses and the overall default rate before and after the loss, assuming the dropped rows were typical of their region. (b) Explain why the checks that passed could not detect the problem. (c) Name three further checks or practices that would have caught it and say what each examines.

rubric.text: Computes an overall loss of 200,000 / 5,000,000 = 4% and a regional loss of 200,000 / 1,000,000 = 20%.
Computes the default rate falling from 4.8% to 4.5% (216,000 of 4,800,000), a shift small enough to pass for ordinary quarter-to-quarter variation.

Explains that checks on nulls, types, ranges and summary statistics examine only the rows present, so a row that never arrived leaves no trace; a passing check shows only that the property tested holds.
Names row reconciliation: compare counts per source, per stage and per group before and after each join or merge against what was expected.

Names two further practices, such as repeating the checks within each subgroup (region), comparing against an independent control total, and plotting distributions by group, together with domain knowledge about what the counts should be.

questions.section: 5. Modeling basics: fit, overfitting and evaluation
questions.prompt: A vendor says its screening model is "99.3% accurate" at flagging a rare condition. On a test set of 100,000 cases, 800 are positive. The model flags 300 cases, of which 200 are truly positive. An alternative model flags 3,000 cases and catches 600 of the positives. (a) Build the confusion matrix for the first model and compute accuracy, precision, recall and F1. (b) Compare it with a trivial baseline. (c) Explain which metrics the decision should rest on, and compare the two models when a missed positive costs 500 and a false alarm costs 10.

rubric.text: Gives TP 200, FP 100, FN 600, TN 99,100 and computes accuracy 99.3%, precision 200/300 ≈ 67%, recall 200/800 = 25% and F1 ≈ 0.36.
Notes that a baseline that flags nothing scores 99,200 / 100,000 = 99.2% accuracy, so 99.3% is barely better than doing no detection, because accuracy is dominated by the majority class.
Explains that the decision should rest on metrics that respect the rare class, such as recall (here 600 of 800 positives are missed), precision and the precision-recall trade-off, not accuracy.

Computes expected cost = 500 × misses + 10 × false alarms: 301,000 for the first model, 124,000 for the alternative (200 misses, 2,400 false alarms) and 400,000 for flagging nothing, so the alternative wins despite lower accuracy (97.4%) and precision (20%).

Explains that the operating point should be chosen to minimize expected cost or meet a recall target on validation data, noting that with calibrated probabilities the cost-minimizing cutoff is 10 / (10 + 500) ≈ 2% and that the deployment base rate matters.

questions.section: 5. Modeling basics: fit, overfitting and evaluation
questions.prompt: A team tunes a classifier by trying 200 hyperparameter configurations and scoring each on the same fixed test set of 500 labeled examples. The best configuration scores 85% accuracy and the team reports "85% expected accuracy in production". Suppose, hypothetically, that all 200 configurations truly have 80% accuracy. (a) Explain why the best score is still expected to exceed 80%, and estimate the size of the effect using the standard error of a single score. (b) Describe a protocol that avoids the problem. (c) List two other ways the 85% could be inflated.

rubric.text: Computes the standard error of one score, √(0.8 × 0.2 / 500) ≈ 1.8 percentage points, so identical configurations still differ by chance.
Explains that taking the maximum of 200 noisy scores selects luck (selection bias, the winner's curse): the expected best of 200 is about 2.7 standard errors above the truth, roughly 84 to 85% here.
States that the test set was used for model selection and is therefore no longer an independent estimate.

Proposes tuning on a separate validation set or by cross-validation (or nested cross-validation), then using the test set once for the chosen model and reporting an interval (about ±3.5 points at 500 examples).

Names two other inflations: leakage from preprocessing or feature selection done on all data before splitting, duplicate or near-duplicate examples across splits, or a test distribution that differs from production.

questions.prompt: A vendor claims that its meeting-summarization assistant "saves our managers time." Explain how you would turn this plausible-sounding claim into an explicit prediction, a list of assumptions, and a falsification test. Give a concrete version of each for this claim, and say what makes the result a test rather than a description.

rubric.text: States a prediction that names a measurable quantity, a defined population and a direction of change, for example minutes per week spent on meeting follow-up for a defined group of managers being lower with the assistant.

Names a comparison or baseline, such as a before-and-after measurement with a control group or a randomized or matched comparison, so that a change can be attributed to the assistant rather than to the calendar.

Lists assumptions that could fail and can be inspected, for example that time is measured from logs and not only from self-report, that managers do not spend the saved time re-checking inaccurate summaries, and that the trial group resembles the managers the claim is meant to cover.

Gives a falsifier fixed in advance with a threshold and a window, such as no reduction of at least a stated number of minutes per week over four weeks, or an increase in correction time, so that a specific result counts against the claim.

Explains that the criteria are set before the results are seen and that a claim compatible with every outcome, such as "saves time" with no baseline or threshold, is not testable because no result could count against it.

questions.prompt: Two reviewers comment on a team's claim that a classifier "generalizes well to new hospitals." Reviewer 1 writes: "I'm not convinced this will hold up in the real world." Reviewer 2 writes: "Evaluate on the three hospitals that were not in the training data, using the same labelling protocol; if AUROC at any of them falls below 0.80, I will treat the claim as refuted." Explain which comment does more for the team and why. Define what makes a falsifier checkable, and say what useful role, if any, a general expression of doubt still plays.

rubric.text: Defines a checkable falsifier as a statement of an observation (data, metric, threshold and procedure) that would count against the particular claim, specific enough that two people would agree on whether it occurred.
Identifies Reviewer 2's comment as meeting this standard because it names a population, a metric, a threshold and a consequence, and notes that the claim could actually fail the test.
Explains that Reviewer 1's comment names no observation, so no result could satisfy it and the team can only respond by asserting confidence; it is compatible with every outcome.
Notes the limits of Reviewer 2's test: passing shows the claim survived this test and not that it holds everywhere, and the threshold, the choice of hospitals and the metric each need justification.

Gives the legitimate role of general doubt as a prompt for generating hypotheses about what could be wrong, such as differences in scanners or patient mix, which then must be converted into specific tests.

questions.prompt: A data scientist trains several model variants, looks at the validation results, and then writes a clear and plausible explanation of why one variant won. A colleague writes down a prediction and a decision rule before running the same comparison. Explain why the colleague's prediction is stronger evidence than the data scientist's explanation even when both agree with the data. Describe the mechanisms that weaken the after-the-fact account and the practical steps that preserve the strength of a prediction.

rubric.text: Explains that an account built after the result can be fitted to whichever outcome occurred (hindsight), so its agreement with the data is guaranteed and carries little information.
Explains that a prediction made beforehand could have been wrong, so its success discriminates between the hypothesis and its alternatives; surviving a risky test is what counts as evidence.

Names the multiple-comparisons or forking-paths problem: many subgroups, metrics or analyses can be examined after seeing the data and some will look significant by chance, for example 20 independent tests at the 5% level give about a 64% chance of at least one hit with no true effect.
Describes practical steps: record the prediction, metric, threshold and analysis plan in a dated record before the run, do not edit it afterward, and append observations separately.
Handles exploratory findings correctly by treating post hoc patterns as hypotheses to test on new data, and by reporting which analyses were planned and which were exploratory.

questions.prompt: An engineer asks an LLM why a deployed model's accuracy fell from 91% to 84% last month. The LLM, which was given only those two numbers, answers with a polished, confident, three-paragraph explanation blaming a "seasonal shift in input vocabulary." The engineer is tempted to report this to management as the cause. Explain what evidence the claim "a seasonal vocabulary shift caused the drop" needs, what the explanation does and does not supply, and how you would test it.

rubric.text: Explains that polished form is not evidence about content, since fluent text can be produced for true and false claims alike, and that the model saw only two numbers so its specifics cannot come from the system's data.

States that a causal claim needs evidence that distinguishes it from alternatives such as a data pipeline change, a labelling change, a shift in class mix, an upstream bug or a change in the evaluation set.

Proposes concrete checks that could contradict the explanation, such as comparing input vocabulary between the two months, breaking errors down by slice, and confirming that labels and metric computation were unchanged.
Proposes an intervention or counterfactual test, such as adapting the model to the new vocabulary and seeing whether accuracy recovers, with the prediction stated before the test is run.
Describes honest reporting: the explanation is an unverified hypothesis until a test supports it, and the report should say what was checked and what was not.

questions.prompt: A team builds a pipeline in which one language model drafts summaries of legal clauses and a second language model, from a different vendor, "verifies" each summary by reading the clause and the summary and replying "correct" or "incorrect." The team reports that the verifier agrees with the drafter on 97% of summaries and concludes that the summaries are verified. Critique this conclusion, and describe how you would build a check whose agreement would mean something.

rubric.text: Notes that agreement between two models measures agreement and not correctness, since neither is ground truth and both can be wrong in the same way.

Explains how shared assumptions weaken independence: overlapping training data, similar architectures and failure modes, the same input read in the same way, and a verifier that sees the drafter's summary and may anchor on it, so their errors are correlated.

Points out that 97% agreement means little without knowing how the verifier performs on summaries known to be wrong, and proposes measuring its sensitivity on a labelled or deliberately corrupted set.

Proposes a check grounded outside the models, such as domain experts reviewing a random sample against the source clause, a labelled dataset with known answers, or programmatic checks that extracted dates, amounts and clause numbers match the source text.

States that independence is a matter of degree that has to be argued, that the check's measured error rates and sample should be reported, and that a named person remains responsible for the conclusion.

questions.prompt: An automation agent reports: "I rotated the API keys for all 14 services and revoked the old ones." A manager is ready to close the security ticket. Explain the difference between the agent's report and the state of the world it describes, then design a verification procedure that does not rely on the agent's own account. Say what that procedure can and cannot establish.

rubric.text: Distinguishes the report, which is something the agent produced and may reflect only that commands were issued or returned success, from the real state of what each service accepts.

Lists ways the report could be wrong, such as services that were missed or silently failed, new keys not deployed to dependent systems, old keys still valid because revocation lagged or failed, and a service list that is itself incomplete.

Designs checks against actual state, such as attempting to authenticate with each old key and confirming rejection, confirming that the new keys work, reading each service's key list or audit log, and reconciling the 14 against an independently maintained inventory.
Notes that the checks draw on sources independent of the agent, such as service-side logs and a separately obtained inventory, and are run against the live system and not a copy or a summary.

States the limits: the checks cover the services and keys examined at the time they were run, copies of old keys or unlisted services remain unaddressed, and the result should be recorded as what was verified and what remains unknown, with a named person closing the ticket.

questions.prompt: A product manager says: "We ran 300 randomly sampled production-like requests through the new triage model and saw zero serious errors. The serious-error rate is zero, so we can ship." The system will handle about 200,000 requests per month. Respond to this argument with appropriate statistical reasoning, including a numerical bound, and say what additional information you would need before deciding.

rubric.text: States that zero observed failures in a finite sample does not establish a zero rate, because no finite sample can confirm that failures are absent.
Gives a quantitative bound: with 0 failures in 300 independent trials, the one-sided 95% upper bound on the failure rate is about 3/300, or 1%.

Translates the bound to volume: a rate of up to 1% across 200,000 monthly requests is consistent with the data and would mean up to about 2,000 serious errors per month, so the decision depends on the tolerable rate and the severity.
Questions representativeness, since the bound holds only for the population sampled and assumes independent trials, and rare subgroups, adversarial inputs and post-launch shift are not covered.

Recommends next steps, such as targeted stress tests aimed at likely failures, a staged rollout with monitoring and a stopping threshold stated in advance, and a stricter requirement where errors are severe.

questions.prompt: A claims department adopts a model that drafts 5,000 decision letters a day. A trained reviewer needs about 6 minutes to check one letter against the claim file. Discuss the relationship between the cost of generating and the cost of verifying outputs like these, why ignoring it creates risk, and how you would design a verification plan under a limited reviewer budget. State the limits of any general claim you make about generating versus verifying costs.

rubric.text: Explains that producing a letter is cheap and fast while checking it requires a trained person reading against the file, and computes that full review would take about 5,000 x 6 minutes, or 500 reviewer-hours per day.

Hedges the principle: for some problems verification is cheaper than production, such as multiplying given factors or running a test, while for others no cheap check exists, so the relationship depends on the task and on whether a ground truth is available.
Explains the risk of not budgeting for checking: unchecked outputs look fine by default, and errors accumulate at scale until they surface as harm.

Designs a plan with risk tiering (full review of high-stakes letters), random sampling with a stated detection target (for example about 150 letters per day to have a 95% chance of catching at least one error when the error rate is 2%), automated checks on fields that can be checked mechanically, and escalation when sampled error rates rise.

Notes that sampling estimates the error rate without verifying the unsampled letters, that the plan should state what is covered and what is not, that a named owner accepts the residual risk, and that using another model to check does not remove the need for a ground-truth anchor.

questions.prompt: A company wants an AI agent to prepare and submit changes to production prices. Management says "a human approves every change," and the plan is a single Approve button shown beside the agent's own summary of the change. Explain what is missing for the approval to carry real responsibility, and design the approval step so that a named person can be accountable for the decision.

rubric.text: Identifies that an approval is meaningful only if the approver sees what will change, such as a concrete before-and-after difference and its scope, and not only the agent's summary of it.
Requires that the approver has the knowledge, the authority to refuse and the time to review, and flags rubber-stamping and over-reliance on automated suggestions when volume is high.

Specifies a named accountable person or role recorded with each decision, so that responsibility does not dissolve into the system, and states that an AI component cannot be held answerable for the choice.

Specifies the evidence shown to the approver: checks run against actual state, such as a preview computed from the real price table, a statement of what was not checked, and how the change can be rolled back, with a record of what was shown, who approved and when.

Explains that the decision to approve, revise or stop stays with the human, including stopping when a check is unknown or fails, and that approval rates, review time and rejection rates are monitored to detect superficial review.

questions.prompt: You evaluated a speech-to-text system for a clinic. You tested it on 120 recordings, all made in a quiet room by 6 native English speakers, and it transcribed 114 correctly (95%) under your scoring rule. You did not test noisy environments, non-native accents, or medical terms beyond a short list. Write the claims you can and cannot support, and explain why a verification report should state what was and was not checked. Include how you would label the status of the untested conditions.

rubric.text: States the supportable claim narrowly: in quiet rooms, with these 6 native speakers and these recordings, 114 of 120 (95%) were transcribed correctly under the stated scoring rule, and notes that so few speakers limits generalization even within that group.
Notes statistical uncertainty: 114 of 120 carries a 95% interval of roughly 90% to 98%, so the figure should not be presented as precise.
Says the untested conditions (noise, accents, vocabulary) must be reported as unknown or not evaluated, not as passing or assumed acceptable, because no failures were seen where nothing was tested.

Explains the purpose: readers will make decisions from the report, omitted limits transfer risk to people who do not know about them, and an honest scope lets others judge whether the evidence applies to their setting.

Recommends a report format with scope, method, sample, criteria fixed beforehand, results, a pass, fail or not-tested status for each condition, and next tests, using wording that does not imply the whole system was verified.

questions.source: What you measure and what you care about
questions.prompt: A hospital system trains a model to rank patients for a care-coordination program, using each patient's past-year healthcare cost as the training label on the reasoning that costlier patients are sicker. Explain how the label can come apart from the goal. Distinguish the two ways a measure and a goal can diverge (a stand-in that never tracked the goal, and a measure that tracked it and later stopped), and describe the checks that address each.

rubric.text: Identifies the measure (cost) and the goal (health need) and explains why cost is only a partial stand-in, since spending depends on access, insurance, referral patterns and treatment intensity, so patients with the same illness can differ in cost.
Names Goodhart's law or proxy optimization: ranking or optimizing on the stand-in can exploit the parts of it that are unrelated to the goal.

Describes divergence from the start (a proxy with weak construct validity) and the pre-deployment check, comparing the label with direct measures of the goal, such as clinical indicators, and comparing groups at the same score.

Describes divergence that opens after deployment, from policy changes, population change or behavior that responds to the measure, and that it is caught only by repeated checks against fresh direct outcome data.

Gives the remedy of changing the label to a quantity closer to the goal, or combining quantities, and states what the replacement costs, such as more data, delay or noise, instead of only patching features.

questions.prompt: A credit-risk model has been accurate for two years, and the team argues that this record shows it will stay accurate. Explain the problem with that argument, then design a post-deployment monitoring plan that would detect when past performance stops predicting future performance. Specify what you would monitor, how you would decide that something is wrong, and what you would do about it.

rubric.text: Explains the induction problem: past success supports future success only if the conditions that produced it persist, no number of past correct predictions guarantees the next, and a stable data distribution is an assumption.

Identifies kinds of shift, including covariate shift (inputs change), concept shift (the relationship between inputs and outcomes changes), population change, and feedback from the model's own decisions.

Monitors inputs against the training or validation data using a stated statistic and threshold, such as the population stability index, as an early warning, and explains that input monitoring does not show that accuracy has fallen.

Monitors outcomes against realized results, by segment and with thresholds and windows set in advance, and notes limits such as the delay before credit outcomes are known and the missing outcomes for applicants who were declined.
Defines actions: alerts to a named owner, human review, a fallback or retraining, a stopping rule, and re-validation after any known change.

questions.prompt: A model trained to detect a disease from chest X-rays reaches 94% accuracy on a held-out test set drawn from the same hospitals as its training data, but only 71% at a new hospital. Explain what might account for the gap, with reference to the difference between what the model's output reports and the clinical reality it is meant to reflect. Describe how you would test your explanations.

rubric.text: Distinguishes the output, a label produced by a statistical model from image pixels, from the thing it is meant to track, disease in the patient, and notes that high held-out accuracy shows only that the label can be predicted from inputs like the training data.

Identifies shortcut learning or spurious correlation: confounders such as scanner type, markers, patient positioning, text tags or hospital-specific prevalence that correlate with the label at the training hospitals but not elsewhere.

Notes that a random held-out split from the same sources shares those confounders and so cannot reveal reliance on them, which is why external validation at a new site or another out-of-distribution test is needed.

Proposes diagnostics that could contradict the shortcut explanation, such as stratifying results by hospital or scanner, masking or cropping the suspect regions, and training a model that sees only the confounding feature to see whether it predicts the label.

Names other candidate causes, such as differences in labelling, in the patient population or disease spectrum, and in image processing, and says each should be tested instead of accepting the first plausible account.

questions.prompt: A team adds an automated AI reviewer that scans pull requests for security flaws. In its first month the reviewer reports no security issues in any of 400 pull requests, and a manager concludes that the code base is secure. Explain what this negative finding does and does not establish, and describe how you would measure whether the reviewer can find the flaws it is supposed to find.

rubric.text: States that "no findings" depends on two things, whether flaws exist and whether the reviewer would detect them, so a clean report is uninformative until the detection rate is known.

Illustrates with numbers or reasoning, for example that a reviewer catching 60% of flaws leaves a 40% chance of a clean report on a flawed pull request, that the probability of a flaw after a clean report depends on the prior flaw rate and the detection rate and is not zero, and that a reviewer unable to detect a class of flaw says nothing about that class.

Proposes measuring sensitivity by seeding known flaws, or replaying known past vulnerabilities, into held-out pull requests and counting how many are flagged by class of flaw, and also measuring the false alarm rate.
Addresses coverage: which languages, files, flaw categories and parts of the change the reviewer examines, with everything outside its scope listed as not checked.

Concludes that the manager's claim goes beyond the evidence and offers a defensible statement of the form "the reviewer flagged none; its measured detection rate on seeded flaws of these classes was X," with human or independent review of the highest-risk code.

questions.prompt: A team uses a language model to grade 200 chatbot answers as pass or fail, and it passes 180 of them (90%). To check the judge, people with domain knowledge relabel a random sample of 50 of the 200 answers. In that sample the judge and the people cross-tabulate as follows: judge pass and human pass, 37; judge pass and human fail, 8; judge fail and human fail, 4; judge fail and human pass, 1. Interpret these results. State what the 90% pass rate does and does not tell you, compute the relevant rates from the table, and recommend what to do next.

rubric.text: States that 90% is the judge's pass rate, a statement by the checking instrument and not a measurement of correctness, which requires an independent reference such as the human labels.
Computes from the table: agreement is 41 of 50 (82%), the humans passed 38 of 50 (76%) against the judge's 90%, and of the 45 judge passes 8 (about 18%) were human fails.
Computes the judge's sensitivity to failures: of the 12 answers the humans failed, the judge flagged 4 (33%), so it is lenient and misses most bad answers, and its errors are not random.

Notes the uncertainty from a sample of 50, with a 95% interval for the human pass rate of roughly 63% to 86%, the need for the sample to be random for any extrapolation, and that human raters can also be checked for agreement with each other.

Recommends reporting the human-labelled estimate with its interval instead of the judge's number, enlarging the labelled sample, studying the kinds of errors the judge accepts, revising the judge and re-measuring its agreement with humans, and keeping a person responsible for decisions that depend on the score.

questions.source: The test that is 99% accurate, and the patient it kills
questions.prompt: A vendor says its fraud-screening tool is "98% accurate", meaning it flags 98% of fraudulent transactions and clears 98% of legitimate ones. In the vendor's target market 0.2% of transactions (1 in 500) are fraudulent. (a) For 100,000 transactions, work out how many are flagged and how many of the flagged transactions are fraudulent. (b) Explain why the vendor's figure and your figure are both correct yet answer different questions. (c) Describe two changes that would raise the share of flags that are real fraud, and one cost of each.

rubric.text: Gets the counts right: 200 fraudulent transactions with 196 flagged, 99,800 legitimate with about 1,996 flagged, about 2,192 flags in total, so only about 8.9% of flags are fraud.

Explains that 98% is P(flag | fraud) and P(clear | legitimate), probabilities conditioned on true status, whereas the question asked is P(fraud | flag), the reverse conditional, which needs the base rate through Bayes' rule.
Explains the mechanism: legitimate transactions outnumber fraud by about 500 to 1, so even a 2% false-positive rate produces about ten false flags for every true one.

Gives two levers with a cost for each, for example raising specificity (99.9% specificity would lift the share to about 66%, at the cost of sensitivity or complexity) or screening a higher-risk subpopulation (at 2% prevalence the share is about 50%, at the cost of missing fraud outside it) or adding a second review stage.

Draws the operational consequence (reviewers see mostly false alarms, leading to alert fatigue and ignored real fraud) and says what to demand from a vendor: separate sensitivity and specificity and the share of flags that are real at a stated prevalence.

questions.prompt: People often treat "accuracy", "discrimination" (for example AUC) and "calibration" as interchangeable ways of saying that a probabilistic classifier is good. (a) Define each of the three. (b) Give a concrete example, in numbers or by construction, of a model that is calibrated but has no discrimination, and of a model with excellent discrimination but poor calibration. (c) For each of two decisions, ranking cases for a limited number of reviewers and quoting a patient a numerical risk, say which property matters most and how you would check it.

rubric.text: Defines accuracy at a threshold as the fraction correct after thresholding, discrimination as the ability to rank positives above negatives (AUC is the probability a random positive outscores a random negative), and calibration as agreement between stated probabilities and observed frequencies.
Gives a calibrated model without discrimination: always predicting the base rate (for example 0.10 at 10% prevalence) matches observed frequency overall but has AUC 0.5.

Gives a discriminating but miscalibrated model: any strictly increasing distortion of a perfect ranker (for example scores between 0.6 and 1.0 at 10% prevalence) keeps AUC at 1.0 while the stated probabilities are far too high.
Notes that accuracy at a threshold discards confidence magnitude, can be high through class imbalance alone (a majority-class baseline), and neither implies nor is implied by calibration or AUC.

Matches properties to decisions with checks: ranking depends on discrimination (AUC or precision at the review capacity); quoting a risk depends on calibration (reliability diagram with counts, Brier score or log loss on data from the deployment population).

questions.prompt: Two forecasters each give a probability for 10 events, 8 of which occur. Forecaster P says 0.8 for every event. Forecaster Q says 0.99 for every event. (a) For each forecaster compute accuracy at a 0.5 cutoff, the Brier score and the log loss (natural logarithm). (b) Define a proper scoring rule and explain why Brier score and log loss are proper while accuracy at a cutoff is not. (c) Explain how Brier score and log loss differ in their treatment of a confident forecast that turns out wrong, and when that should influence the choice between them.

rubric.text: Finds that accuracy at 0.5 is 0.8 for both forecasters, so it cannot distinguish the calibrated forecaster from the overconfident one.
Computes Brier scores of 0.160 for P and about 0.196 for Q, and log losses of about 0.500 for P and about 0.929 for Q, so P is better on both.
Defines a proper scoring rule as one whose expected score is optimized by reporting one's true belief (strictly proper if only that report is optimal).

Explains that Brier score and log loss are proper (honest reporting of 0.8 is optimal when 80% of events occur) while accuracy at a cutoff rewards any report on the right side of 0.5 equally, so it neither rewards honesty nor penalizes overstatement; absolute error is also not proper.

Contrasts the penalty for a confident miss: a single wrong forecast of 0.99 costs 0.98 in Brier score (bounded by 1) but about 4.6 in log loss, which is unbounded as the probability given to the outcome approaches 0, so log loss suits settings where confident errors are very costly and Brier score is less dominated by single extreme errors.

questions.prompt: A classifier's predicted probabilities on 1,000 test cases are grouped into five bins. For each bin the table gives the number of cases, the mean predicted probability and the observed fraction of positives: (300, 0.10, 0.13), (200, 0.30, 0.38), (200, 0.50, 0.47), (150, 0.70, 0.58), (150, 0.90, 0.72). (a) Compute the expected calibration error (ECE) and the maximum calibration error. (b) Describe in words what pattern the table shows. (c) Show that the ECE depends on how the bins are drawn by recomputing it with a single bin for all 1,000 cases, and give further reasons an ECE figure alone should not decide whether a model is acceptable.

rubric.text: Computes the ECE as the count-weighted mean absolute gap, 0.3 x 0.03 + 0.2 x 0.08 + 0.2 x 0.03 + 0.15 x 0.12 + 0.15 x 0.18 = 0.076, and the maximum calibration error as 0.18.

Reads the pattern: low probabilities are understated (observed rates above predictions at 0.10 and 0.30) and high probabilities are overstated (observed rates well below predictions at 0.70 and 0.90), so the probabilities are too extreme, with clear overconfidence at the top.
Shows binning dependence: with one bin the mean prediction is 0.43 and the observed rate 0.404, so ECE falls to 0.026 because gaps of opposite sign cancel; merging bins can only keep or lower ECE.

Notes sampling noise: each bin's observed rate has a standard error of roughly 0.02 to 0.04 at these counts, and even a perfectly calibrated model has a positive expected ECE at finite sample size that grows with the number of bins.

Recommends complements: a reliability diagram with bin counts and intervals, Brier score or log loss, equal-count bins as a check, subgroup and time slices, and attention to the probability range that drives decisions rather than a single pass-fail threshold on ECE.

questions.prompt: A team asks a language model to answer 1,000 factual questions and to append "Confidence: N%" to each answer. The team wants to know whether those percentages can be treated as the probability that the answer is correct. Design the evaluation: what data and labels to collect, how to analyze them, what sample size issues and sources of error matter, and what the results would and would not let you conclude.

rubric.text: Establishes an independent ground truth for each answer (graded against verified references, with a plan for ambiguous items) so that the stated confidence is compared with real correctness rather than with the model's own judgment.

Collects (stated confidence, correct or not) pairs, groups them by stated value (noting that verbalized numbers cluster at a few round values), computes the observed accuracy for each group, and examines a reliability diagram, a calibration error and a proper score such as Brier score or log loss.

Addresses sample size and variability: enough cases per group to give intervals narrow enough to be informative, repeated runs because outputs can vary, and fixed, recorded prompt wording and settings with a check of sensitivity to rewording.

Separates discrimination from calibration (does higher stated confidence track higher accuracy, for example by AUC for correct versus incorrect) and compares against baselines such as a constant base-rate accuracy or confidence derived from token probabilities or agreement across samples.

States the limits of any conclusion: results hold for this model version, prompt format and question distribution; they do not carry over to other domains or versions without re-checking; any recalibration map fitted on one set of questions must be validated on fresh questions.

questions.source: When the Central Limit Theorem politely declines to help
questions.prompt: An engineer writes: "We timed 25 requests. The mean was 100 ms and the standard deviation was 15 ms. The 95% interval is 93.8 to 106.2 ms, so there is a 95% chance that the next request will take between 93.8 and 106.2 ms." (a) Identify what the interval actually describes and what is wrong with the conclusion. (b) Compute the interval that does answer the engineer's question, assuming roughly normal times; the t critical value with 24 degrees of freedom is 2.064. (c) Explain how a Bayesian credible interval differs from both.

rubric.text: Identifies 93.8 to 106.2 as the 95% confidence interval for the population mean, 100 plus or minus 2.064 x 15 / sqrt(25), which expresses uncertainty about the average and not the spread of individual requests.
Explains the error in the conclusion: individual requests vary with a standard deviation of 15 ms, so only about a third of them (roughly 32%) would fall inside that narrow range.

Computes the prediction interval, 100 plus or minus 2.064 x 15 x sqrt(1 + 1/25), about 68.4 to 131.6 ms, and notes that it does not shrink to zero with more data because individual variability remains.

States the correct frequentist meaning of the confidence level: across repeated samples the method captures the true mean 95% of the time, which is not the probability that this computed interval contains it and not a statement about the next observation.

Explains that a credible interval is a posterior probability statement about the parameter given a model and prior, depends on the prior, and can resemble the confidence interval only under diffuse priors; notes that all of these assume independent, roughly normal, stable measurements.

questions.source: When the Central Limit Theorem politely declines to help
questions.prompt: A team reports "our classifier is 96% accurate" after it classified 48 of 50 test items correctly, and says this beats a competitor's published figure of 92%, which came from a different, larger test set. (a) Give an approximate 95% interval for the team's true accuracy and say whether the data support the claim. (b) Roughly how many test items would be needed to estimate accuracy to within plus or minus 2 percentage points if the true accuracy is near 96%? (c) Name two sources of error that no sampling interval accounts for.

rubric.text: Computes an interval of roughly 86% to 99% (Wilson about 0.865 to 0.989; exact about 0.863 to 0.995) and notes that the competitor's 92% lies inside it.

Concludes that the data do not establish superiority: 96% is a point estimate from 50 items with wide uncertainty, a four-point gap is within sampling noise, and the competitor's figure has its own uncertainty and a different test set.

Sizes the test: n is about 1.96 squared x 0.96 x 0.04 / 0.02 squared, roughly 370 items (about 1,480 for plus or minus 1 point); interval width falls with the square root of n, and with unknown accuracy the conservative figure is about 2,400.

Names non-sampling errors such as an unrepresentative test set, near-duplicate items or leakage from training data, label noise, choosing the model or threshold after seeing the test set, and shift between test data and deployment.
Proposes a better comparison design: evaluate both systems on the same items and analyze paired differences with an interval, with the test set and metric fixed in advance.

questions.source: From Boolean to probabilistic — and why the move is harder than it looks
questions.prompt: A loan-approval vendor's dashboard shows each applicant's "probability of repayment" to one decimal place, for example 92.7%, and the vendor argues that this precision shows the model is rigorous. Evaluate the argument. Say what evidence would be needed before an analyst treated 92.7% as a probability, and what else the analyst should check before relying on it to make decisions.

rubric.text: Argues that displayed precision is a formatting choice and says nothing about validity: any model can print any number of digits, and the real uncertainty (sampling error, model error) is far larger than the last digit.

Explains that the number means something only if it is calibrated: among past applicants scored near 92.7%, about 93% repaid, shown by a reliability diagram or calibration error computed from labeled outcomes.
Requires that the evidence come from data resembling the current applicant population and period, and that calibration be rechecked over time because base rates and inputs shift.

Asks for supporting detail: how many cases lie behind each score range (a claim near 92.7% needs enough cases), a proper score such as Brier score or log loss compared with a trivial baseline, and calibration within subgroups rather than only in aggregate.

Looks beyond the probability to the decision: the costs of approving a loan that defaults versus declining one that would repay, and the possibility of rare, very large losses that an average figure hides.

questions.prompt: A disease has prevalence 0.1%. A diagnostic test has sensitivity 95% and specificity 95%. (a) A person chosen at random from the screened population tests positive. What is the probability that they have the disease? Show your reasoning with counts or Bayes' rule. (b) The test is repeated and is positive again. Under what assumption can you update by multiplying likelihood ratios, and what is the new probability? (c) Describe a realistic situation in which that assumption fails and say what follows for the posterior. (d) What would you recommend after a first positive result?

rubric.text: Gets the first-positive probability of about 1.9% using counts (per 100,000 people: 95 true positives and 4,995 false positives) or Bayes' rule, and explains that the low base rate dominates.

Updates correctly: the posterior from the first result becomes the prior for the second, each positive multiplies the odds by the likelihood ratio 0.95 / 0.05 = 19, and two positives give about 27% (three would give about 87%).
States the assumption needed: the two results are conditionally independent given the person's true status, so errors are not shared.

Gives a case where it fails (the same specimen, the same assay or the same interfering substance causing both false positives) and explains that the second positive is then much less informative than independence implies, so the posterior is overstated.

Recommends confirmation with a test that works by a different mechanism, rather than interpreting a single screening positive as a diagnosis, and notes that treating accuracy as the probability of disease (for example 95% x 95%) ignores the prior.

questions.prompt: In a court case an expert testifies: "The chance that an innocent person would match this DNA profile is 1 in 100,000, so the chance that the defendant is innocent is 1 in 100,000." The defendant was identified by searching a database that covers all 1,000,000 possible sources, each equally likely beforehand, and the true source is one of them. Identify the error in the testimony, compute the probability that the defendant is the source given the match, and explain what the match does establish. Then explain why the same error appears when people read automated alerts.

rubric.text: Identifies the transposed conditional: 1 in 100,000 is P(match | innocent), whereas the court needs P(innocent | match), and the two are different quantities that need the prior to connect.
Computes that about 10 innocent people in 1,000,000 are expected to match by chance, alongside the one true source.
Applies Bayes' rule with a prior of 1 in 1,000,000 to get a probability that the defendant is the source of about 1 in 11, roughly 0.09.

Explains that the match is still strong evidence (a likelihood ratio of about 100,000 raised the probability from 0.000001 to 0.09) and that with other independent evidence the same match could give a probability near certainty.

Generalizes: reading an alert's false-positive rate as the probability that a flagged case is harmless, or its detection rate as the probability that a flagged case is real, makes the same error and requires the base rate.

questions.prompt: A neural network classifier assigns probability 0.95 to its predicted class on a validation set, but is correct on only 80% of those cases. (a) Is this overconfidence or underconfidence, and how would you display it? (b) Temperature scaling replaces the predicted probability sigma(z), where z is the logit and sigma the logistic function, by sigma(z / T) for a single T fitted on held-out data. Show what happens to a case with logit z = 3 when T = 2, and find the T that maps it to 0.80. (c) Explain what temperature scaling cannot change and when the fix fails.

rubric.text: Identifies overconfidence (stated 0.95 above observed 0.80) and says it appears as a reliability diagram point below the diagonal at high confidence.
Describes temperature scaling as dividing logits by one parameter T fitted on held-out data (typically minimizing log loss), with T > 1 softening probabilities toward 0.5.
Computes the example: sigma(3) is about 0.953, sigma(1.5) with T = 2 is about 0.818, and T of about 2.16 gives 0.80.
Explains that dividing by T preserves the ordering of cases, so predicted classes, accuracy and AUC (in the binary case) are unchanged and only the stated confidence is rescaled.

States the limits: it fits average calibration on the data it was fitted on; one parameter cannot fix class-specific or subgroup miscalibration or a shifted population; it must be fitted on data separate from the evaluation set and rechecked over time.

questions.source: Synthesis — four questions that prevent most deployment disasters
questions.prompt: A hospital can follow up flagged patients at $20 each. A missed positive costs $400. A model sorts 1,000 patients into three groups with calibrated probabilities: group 1 has 700 patients with positive rate 0.01, group 2 has 200 patients with positive rate 0.06, and group 3 has 100 patients with positive rate 0.30. (a) Derive the probability cutoff that minimizes expected cost. (b) Compute the expected total cost per 1,000 patients of four policies: follow up nobody, follow up group 3 only, follow up groups 2 and 3, and follow up everyone. (c) Explain why a 0.5 cutoff is the wrong choice here. (d) Suppose group 2's true positive rate is actually 0.03 although the model still reports 0.06. What is the consequence, and what does it show about the role of calibration?

rubric.text: Derives the cutoff: follow up when the expected cost of missing, 400p, exceeds the follow-up cost 20, so p > 20 / 420, about 0.048.
Computes the costs: nobody $19,600, group 3 only $9,600, groups 2 and 3 $8,800, everyone $20,000, so following up groups 2 and 3 is best.

Explains that no group has a probability above 0.5, so a 0.5 cutoff follows up nobody and costs $19,600, more than double the optimum, because a criterion that counts errors equally ignores that a miss costs twenty times a follow-up.

Shows the effect of miscalibration: with group 2's true rate at 0.03, following up groups 2 and 3 costs $8,800 while following up group 3 alone costs $7,200, a waste of $1,600 (about 22%), so a cost-derived cutoff is only valid if the stated probabilities equal true frequencies.

Notes that the cutoff and the best policy move with the cost ratio and the base rate, so costs and prevalence should be examined for uncertainty and calibration rechecked on deployment data and by subgroup.

questions.source: Hume's induction problem, re-translated as distribution shift
questions.prompt: A screening classifier was validated at a prevalence of 20% and found to have sensitivity 90% and specificity 90%. It is later deployed in a population where the prevalence is 2%. (a) Compute the share of flagged cases that are truly positive at each prevalence. (b) Explain what changed and what did not, and whether the model got worse. (c) Explain why the model's own output scores would not alert anyone to the problem. (d) Describe the kinds of shift that can occur and a monitoring plan that would catch them, relating this to the general limits of relying on a past track record.

rubric.text: Computes about 0.69 at 20% prevalence (per 1,000 cases: 180 true positives and 80 false positives) and about 0.155 at 2% (18 true positives and 98 false positives).

Explains that sensitivity and specificity are unchanged while the prior changed, so the model did not degrade as a classifier but its flags are now mostly false, and any probability score tied to the old prior is now too high.

Explains that a score is computed from the inputs under assumptions learned in training and does not itself register a change in the population, so scores and dashboards can look unchanged while real-world performance falls.

Names kinds of shift with an example of each, such as prior (base-rate) shift, covariate shift in the inputs, concept drift in the relationship between inputs and outcomes, and changes in how measurements are made.

Proposes monitoring: track realized outcomes on a labeled sample, watch input distributions, recompute calibration and the share of flags that are real over time, recalibrate or re-weight priors, and state the conditions a track record depended on, since past performance supports predictions only while those conditions hold.

questions.prompt: An autonomous agent ends each task by reporting "complete". In the current task mix, 70% of tasks truly succeed. The agent reports "complete" on 98% of the tasks that succeed and on 60% of the tasks that fail. (a) Given that the agent reports "complete", what is the probability that the task actually succeeded? (b) How does the answer change on a harder task mix in which only 30% of tasks succeed? (c) What would the agent's false-"complete" rate on failed tasks need to be for the report to be strong evidence of success, say above 95% at the 70% base rate? (d) How would you measure these quantities in practice?

rubric.text: Interprets the likelihood ratio 0.98 / 0.6, about 1.6: the report moves belief only from 0.70 to 0.79 because failed tasks also end with "complete", so the report is weak evidence of success.
Shows the dependence on the base rate: with 30% of tasks succeeding the same report gives only about 0.41, so the report should not be trusted on hard tasks.

Shows what makes a report informative: the false-"complete" rate would need to fall to about 12% or lower to exceed 95% (at 10% the probability is about 0.96), meaning the report must distinguish success from failure.

Describes measurement: check outcomes independently of the agent's report on a sample, estimate both conditional rates including the rate on failures, give intervals for them, and stratify by task difficulty and by number of steps.

questions.source: When the Central Limit Theorem politely declines to help
questions.prompt: A deployed model's mistakes have this cost distribution: 99.9% of mistakes cost $1 and 0.1% cost $5,000, independently of each other. An audit samples 500 mistakes, finds that every one cost $1, and reports: "average cost per mistake is $1.00 with no variation, so our estimate is precise." (a) Compute the true mean cost and the probability that a 500-mistake audit shows no catastrophic mistake. (b) Explain what is wrong with the team's confidence, and what the central limit theorem does and does not guarantee here. (c) What should the team report instead? Include the bound on the catastrophic-mistake rate that 0 events in 500 supports.

rubric.text: Computes the true mean as about $6.00 (0.999 x $1 + 0.001 x $5,000) and the probability of no $5,000 mistake in 500 as 0.999 to the power 500, about 0.61 (the expected number of catastrophic mistakes is only 0.5).
Explains that a sample with no variation gives a zero-width interval, but the absence of rare events in a sample is not their absence in the population, so the apparent precision is an artifact.

States what the central limit theorem requires (independent observations with finite variance) and notes that convergence can be very slow when rare large values dominate the mean, so a sample must be large relative to 1 divided by the rare event's probability, and that with infinite variance the mean does not stabilize at all.

Gives the bound: 0 events in 500 supports only an upper limit of about 3/500 = 0.6% (about 95% confidence) on the catastrophic rate, six times the true 0.1% rate, which would correspond to an expected cost near $30 per mistake.

Recommends tail-aware reporting and design: report the frequency and size of the largest losses and high quantiles rather than only the mean, use scenario or worst-case analysis, and use targeted or stratified sampling and adversarial testing to find rare severe cases.

questions.source: Reconstructing the epistemic frame — a working procedure
questions.prompt: A data team builds a modeling table by joining three source systems on a shared identifier. An automated report on the result shows no missing values, sensible histograms and no outliers. After deployment, the model performs noticeably worse for one customer segment. Explain how a table with no empty cells can still misrepresent the population it is meant to describe, name the check that would have exposed the problem, and say what that check cannot tell you.

rubric.text: Explains that rows excluded before or during assembly (by a join, filter or gap in a source) are absent rather than blank, so cell-level checks such as missing-value counts have nothing to flag.

Explains that the excluded rows need not be random: if they concentrate in one segment (for example because of inconsistent identifiers), the table under-represents that segment and the model is trained on a different population from the one it serves.
Names row reconciliation: compare the row count of each source with the count after every join, filter or deduplication step, and compare counts per segment before and after.

States that the expected count has to come from outside the file (documentation, source systems or the business definition of the population), because a count is meaningful only against what was supposed to be there.

States the limits: reconciliation shows that rows are missing and where, not why; it cannot show that the surviving rows are accurately measured, or that populations absent from every source are covered.

questions.source: Reconstructing the epistemic frame — a working procedure
questions.prompt: Two tables, orders and customers, will be joined on customer_id and the result used to train a model. Specify the audit report you would require before anyone uses the joined table: what it measures, what would trigger a flag and why, and what must be decided in advance about duplicate keys. Then say what the audit cannot establish even if every check passes.

rubric.text: Reports key uniqueness in each table and requires a decision in advance on whether duplicate keys are an error or an intended one-to-many relationship, because duplicate keys multiply rows.
Reports unmatched keys on both sides (orders with no customer, customers with no order), since the two directions of loss have different meanings.

Reports row counts before and after for the chosen join type and requires any difference to be explained (an inner join drops unmatched rows, a left join keeps them with blanks, duplicates inflate the count).

Reports drop rates per group (region, period, segment) and flags on the worst group or on divergence from the overall rate, justifying this by the fact that a small overall loss can hide a large loss in a subgroup.

States the limits: passing shows only that the join is consistent with its inputs; it does not show that the sources were complete, that matching keys refer to the same entity, or that the values are accurate, which needs external expected counts and domain knowledge.

questions.source: Hidden assumptions that hide in plain sight
questions.prompt: A company runs an opt-in poll on its own website and finds that 82% of respondents say they would buy a new product. It wants to announce that '82% of consumers would buy it'. Using the ideas of target population, sampling frame and self-selection, critique the claim. Explain whether collecting more responses or weighting respondents by age and income would fix it, and say what evidence would make the claim more credible.

rubric.text: Distinguishes the target population (all consumers), the frame (people who visit the site and see the poll) and the respondents (those who choose to answer), identifying coverage and self-selection as separate gaps.
Explains that those who visit and answer are likely more interested in the company and product than typical consumers, so the bias is tied to the outcome and has a likely direction (upward).
Explains that more responses from the same process reduce random error but not systematic bias, so a larger sample gives a more precise wrong answer.

Explains that weighting by observed variables such as age and income corrects composition only if respondents resemble non-respondents within each weighting cell; it cannot correct selection on interest itself and it increases variance.

Proposes stronger evidence: a probability sample from a frame that covers the target population, follow-up of non-respondents with response rates reported, and attention to the gap between stated intention and actual purchase.

questions.source: The procedural EDA pass — what it sees, and what it structurally cannot
questions.prompt: A dataset of 20,000 loan applicants has an income column with 18% of values blank. A missingness plot shows that blanks are far more common among applicants under 25, while the blank rate does not differ noticeably by region or loan size. (a) Which of MCAR, MAR and MNAR is most consistent with this pattern, and why can the pattern not settle the question? (b) Describe a handling strategy that fits your answer and one that would bias the results. (c) What would you do to probe the possibility of MNAR?

rubric.text: Defines the mechanisms (MCAR independent of everything, MAR dependent on observed data, MNAR dependent on the missing value itself) and says that dependence on age, an observed variable, rules out MCAR and is consistent with MAR.

Explains that the observed data cannot distinguish MAR from MNAR, because whether blanks depend on income itself (within age groups) involves values that were not recorded, so the assumption must be argued from how income was collected.

Proposes a handling strategy consistent with MAR, such as multiple or model-based imputation using age and other predictors (or analysis stratified by age), with the uncertainty carried through to the results.
Names a biased alternative, such as dropping all blank rows or filling with the overall mean, which ignores that missingness depends on age, distorts the under-25 group and shrinks variance.

Describes MNAR probes: ask the data owner how income was collected and who skips it, compare with an external source for a subsample, follow up on a sample of non-responders, and run a sensitivity analysis under different assumptions about the missing incomes.

questions.prompt: A team must treat a numeric predictor that has 15% blank values before fitting a regression. They are choosing among (i) dropping rows with any blank, (ii) filling blanks with the column mean, and (iii) multiple imputation. Compare the three: what each assumes about why values are missing, what each does to the mean, the spread, relationships with other variables and the reported uncertainty, and when you would choose each. Say what you would report to readers.

rubric.text: States that dropping rows (complete-case analysis) is unbiased under MCAR but loses data and precision, and is biased when missingness depends on the values or on other variables that matter to the analysis.

States that mean filling assumes MCAR, leaves the mean unchanged but shrinks the variance and attenuates correlations and coefficients, and gives standard errors that are too small because filled values are treated as observed.

States that multiple imputation assumes MAR given the variables in the imputation model, draws several plausible values, analyzes each completed dataset and pools the results so the uncertainty includes imputation variability.

Gives choice guidance: complete-case is acceptable for a small MCAR fraction; multiple imputation suits MAR with informative auxiliary variables; none of the three is sufficient if the mechanism is MNAR, which calls for sensitivity analysis and domain reasoning.
Specifies reporting: the share missing in each column, the assumed mechanism and why, the method used, how many rows were affected, and results under at least one alternative treatment.

questions.source: Hidden assumptions that hide in plain sight
questions.prompt: A team trains a content-moderation classifier on 50,000 posts, each labeled once as harmful or not harmful by a crowd worker. In a pilot, two workers independently label the same 500 posts and obtain a Cohen's kappa of 0.55. Explain what this number says, how the disagreement should affect the way the team trains the model and, especially, how it evaluates it, and what steps they should take to improve label quality.

rubric.text: Explains that kappa measures agreement beyond what chance would produce and that 0.55 is only moderate, so a substantial share of labels are inconsistent.

Notes that disagreement can come from ambiguous guidelines, genuinely ambiguous posts, annotator error or legitimate differences in judgment, and that telling these apart requires reading the disagreements, not just the statistic.

Explains the evaluation consequence: scoring against single noisy labels depresses measured accuracy and compresses differences between models, and a model cannot be shown to beat the level of human agreement, so test labels deserve more care than training labels.

Names training and labeling remedies: several labels per item with aggregation or soft labels, adjudication of disagreements, clearer guidelines with examples, annotator training and gold-standard check items.

Specifies reporting: agreement by category and annotator group, the guideline and annotator pool used, and uncertainty in the evaluation, with attention to whether disagreement is systematic for particular groups or topics.

questions.source: Hidden assumptions that hide in plain sight
questions.prompt: A model that predicts hospital readmission reports 0.98 AUC on its held-out set, while published models for the same task reach about 0.70. Describe at least four distinct ways in which the evaluation could be inflated by information unavailable in deployment or by overlap between training and test data. For each, give a check that would confirm or rule it out, and say what you would conclude if the score drops sharply once the problem is fixed.

rubric.text: Target leakage: a feature recorded after or caused by the outcome (such as a follow-up appointment flag); the check is comparing each feature's timestamp with the prediction time and ablating or inspecting the most influential features.
Entity overlap: several rows per patient fall on both sides of the split; the check is counting shared patient identifiers and re-splitting by patient.
Duplicates and near-duplicates across the split; the check is exact and fuzzy matching between test and training rows or nearest-neighbor distances.

Procedure leakage: scaling, imputation, feature selection or target encoding fitted on all data before splitting, or hyperparameters tuned on the test set; the check is reading the pipeline order and confirming the test set is used once.

Time leakage from a random split of temporal data, checked by a split in which training precedes testing; concludes that a sharp drop means the original figure was an artifact and the lower number is the credible estimate.

questions.source: Hidden assumptions that hide in plain sight
questions.prompt: A school district builds a model to identify students who need extra academic support. Because 'need' is hard to measure, the training label is whether the student received a failing grade the next term.
