Explain the difference between a measurement and the construct it stands for, give at least two ways this label can diverge from need, describe how you could test the size of the gap, and say what high accuracy on the label does and does not show.

rubric.text: Distinguishes the construct (need for support) from the recorded measurement (a failing grade), which is also shaped by grading practices, attendance, course difficulty and interventions already given.
Gives a divergence in which students who need support are labeled 0, for example students who struggle but pass or who are already receiving support.
Gives a divergence in which the label is 1 for reasons other than need for academic support, or in which the relationship between need and label differs across schools or groups.
Describes a test of the gap: compare the label with an independent measure of need (assessments, counselor review of a sample) and compare agreement by school or group.

States that high accuracy shows the model predicts the proxy well, not that the proxy measures need, and that acting on it can reproduce existing grading patterns; suggests multiple indicators, human review or redefining the label.

questions.source: Hidden assumptions that hide in plain sight
questions.prompt: A fraud model was trained on transactions from 2019 to 2021 and deployed in 2024, and its alert precision has been declining. Explain the assumption behind training on that window, distinguish covariate shift, concept drift and a change in the base rate, say how each can be detected, and propose a monitoring and retraining plan, including a difficulty in getting labels to evaluate the live model.

rubric.text: States the assumption that the process generating future data resembles the process that generated the training window, and that a dataset is a snapshot of one period, not a permanent description.

Distinguishes covariate shift (input distribution changes, detectable without labels by comparing feature distributions), concept drift (the input-output relationship changes, seen as lower performance on labeled data) and base-rate change (prevalence of fraud shifts).
Proposes monitoring of input distributions, score distributions, alert volume and performance over time, by segment, with thresholds that trigger an investigation.

Identifies the label difficulty: fraud labels arrive late (for example through chargebacks) and exist mainly for transactions that were flagged or investigated, so live performance is measured with delay and selection bias; mitigates with audited random samples.

Proposes a retraining plan: scheduled and triggered retraining on recent data, validation that trains on earlier periods and tests on later ones, and recording the training window with each model version.

questions.source: Hidden assumptions that hide in plain sight
questions.prompt: A data engineer reports: 'The data passed validation. Every column has the right type, no value is null, and all values are within their allowed ranges.' Explain why this does not establish that the data are correct, give four concrete kinds of error that can pass such checks, and describe the additional checks that would find them.

rubric.text: Distinguishes validity (conforming to declared formats and ranges) from correctness (corresponding to what actually happened), and says schema checks test only the former.
Gives sentinel or default values (0, -999, 1900-01-01) that are valid in type and range, found by looking for spikes in frequency tables and checking the meaning of special values.
Gives unit, scale or encoding mismatches between sources (kilograms and pounds, cents and dollars, time zones), found by comparing distributions by source.
Gives cross-field, temporal or duplicate inconsistencies (discharge before admission, totals that do not add up, stale or repeated records), found by relational rules and duplicate checks.

Gives plausible-but-wrong entries or missing populations, found by tracing sampled records to their source, comparing with an independent source and running checks per group, and records which checks were and were not run.

questions.source: Hidden assumptions that hide in plain sight
questions.prompt: A lender wants to train a default-prediction model. Repayment outcomes exist only for applicants who were approved under an old scoring rule, but the new model will score every applicant. Explain what is wrong with training and evaluating on the approved applicants alone, and describe at least three ways the lender could reduce the problem, including what each one assumes or costs.

rubric.text: Explains that the training sample was selected using a variable related to the outcome, so the model learns relationships only within the approved range and the approved default rate is not the default rate of applicants.
Explains that evaluation on approved loans overstates reliability for the full applicant pool because the rejected region is untested and any extrapolation is an assumption.
Notes that the missing outcomes depend on the old score, so there is no data in the rejected range to adjust from, and statistical adjustment relies on extrapolation.

Names remedies with their price or assumption: randomly approving a small share below the cutoff (costly, but unbiased), reject-inference methods (rest on untestable assumptions), external performance data on rejected applicants, bounds or sensitivity analysis.

Says that, whatever is done, the model's claims should be limited to the population it was validated on, and its performance monitored after launch, particularly on applicants who would previously have been rejected.

questions.source: Hidden assumptions that hide in plain sight
questions.prompt: Your team inherits a training table from another group. One column, customer_value, has no blanks and a clean distribution, and the documentation says only that it was 'computed upstream'. Describe the questions you would ask about this column before using it as a model input, what you would do if the source systems cannot be reached, and how a datasheet for the table would help the next team.

rubric.text: Asks what produced the column: a raw measurement or the output of a model or formula, who built it, from which inputs, parameters, version and date, and whether it can be reproduced.
Asks whether information that exists only at or after the outcome time went into it, and what time window defined it, so its availability at prediction time can be checked.
Asks about stability and ownership: whether upstream owners can recompute or change it, how its assumptions could drift, and what happens to the model if it changes silently.
If the sources are unreachable, records the opacity as a finding, treats the column as unverified, tests sensitivity by modeling with and without it, and checks its behavior by group and over time.
Explains that a datasheet records motivation, composition, collection, preprocessing, uses and maintenance, so the next team can see what was assumed, while not guaranteeing correctness.

questions.source: Reconstructing the epistemic frame — a working procedure
questions.prompt: You present a data validation report to a deployment review board. The automated exploratory report is clean: no missing values, reasonable distributions, no outliers. Your own investigation found that the training data include only customers who completed onboarding, while the deployed model will also score customers who abandoned onboarding partway. A board member asks, 'The report is clean, so why is that not enough to approve?' Write the response you would give, including what you are and are not claiming and what evidence or changes you would ask for.

rubric.text: Explains that the clean report shows the recorded rows are well formed and plausible, not that they represent the population on which the model will run.
Names the selection gap: completers are a filtered subset, abandoners may differ in features and outcomes, so performance on them is untested and could be worse, in an unknown direction.
Asks for the size of the abandoned segment in deployment, the share of decisions it affects and the cost of errors there, so the risk is sized instead of assumed.

Asks for evidence or a change: label and evaluate a sample of abandoners (for example in a pilot or shadow mode), or restrict the model's scope so those customers are routed to review, with monitoring by segment.

States what was and was not checked (types, missingness, ranges and outliers done; coverage of the deployment population and label validity not) and gives a conditional recommendation, not a bare yes or no.

questions.prompt: An engineer proposes giving an AI coding assistant read access to the source databases and letting it carry out the whole data audit for a new modeling project, including writing the dataset documentation. Decide which parts of a data audit you would delegate with light checking, which you would delegate but verify, and which you would keep with a human, giving reasons based on how errors in each part would show up. Respond to the objection that a sufficiently capable assistant could do all of it.

rubric.text: Places mechanical, checkable computations (row counts, type and range checks, missingness tables, histograms, outlier flags, duplicate counts) in the delegate category, because errors show in the output and rerunning is cheap.

Places interpretations (why values are missing, whether a distribution is normal for the domain, suggested imputation, explanations of anomalies) in the verify category, since they read plausibly but depend on collection context that must be confirmed with data owners or tests.

Keeps with a human the decisions about what the dataset is supposed to represent, what the expected counts are, which populations matter and what risk is acceptable, which depend on purpose and stakes and not on computation.
Notes that fluent documentation can look complete without containing information the human did not supply, so style is not evidence and conclusions need independent checks.

Answers the objection by separating capability from verification: access to systems does not reveal undocumented upstream decisions, the intended population or the stakes, independent checking remains needed, and the delegable set may grow as tools improve.

questions.source: A chart is an argument — and the argument is in the encoding
questions.prompt: A validation report for a tabular dataset consists of histograms of each numeric column, a table of missing-value counts, a correlation heatmap of the numeric columns, and a line chart of record counts by month. For each of these four, explain what it can reveal and one specific thing it cannot. Then explain why a heatmap is a poor way to judge whether a correlation of 0.43 differs from 0.51, and what you would use instead.

rubric.text: Histograms can reveal shape, spikes at sentinel values, impossible values and bimodality, but cannot explain why a shape arises or show which rows are absent or how the sample was selected.
Missing-value counts reveal blanks per column but cannot reveal rows excluded before the file existed, or the mechanism (MCAR, MAR or MNAR) that produced the blanks.

A correlation heatmap reveals strong linear association but misses nonlinear dependence (y = x^2 over a symmetric range gives a correlation near zero), can be driven by outliers and says nothing about causation.
A line chart of record counts reveals gaps, drops and level shifts, but cannot identify the cause (outage or real change) or the affected subgroup without breaking the counts down by source or group.

Explains that color intensity is decoded less accurately than position along a common scale, so small differences are hard to judge; uses a scatter plot, a sorted bar or dot chart, or the printed values instead.

questions.prompt: A linear classifier scores an input x with s(x) = w·x + b over d input values, and an attacker may change each value by at most ε in either direction (an L∞ budget). (a) Derive the largest change in the score the attacker can cause and say which change achieves it. (b) Explain, with a numerical example, why small changes to each value can matter more as the number of input values grows, and what this suggests for deep networks that are only piecewise linear. (c) State one thing this linear picture does not explain about adversarial vulnerability.

rubric.text: States that the change in score is w·δ and that, with |δ_i| ≤ ε, it is maximized by δ_i = ε·sign(w_i), giving a largest change of ε·Σ|w_i| = ε‖w‖₁.

Explains that Σ|w_i| grows with the number of input values when typical weight magnitude is fixed, so a change tiny in every coordinate can add up to a decisive shift, with a correct numerical example (for instance d = 1000, |w_i| = 0.02, ε = 0.01 gives 0.2).

Contrasts with a random direction of the same length, where contributions largely cancel and the typical shift is smaller by a factor of about √d, or notes that an attacker limited by Euclidean length r gains at most r‖w‖₂ rather than ε‖w‖₁.

Extends the argument to piecewise-linear networks: they are locally linear, so the sign of the input gradient of the loss gives an effective direction, a one-step gradient-sign attack uses it, and iterating with projection gives stronger attacks.

Names a limit of the linear account, such as that it does not explain why some models trained on the same data are more vulnerable than others, why perturbations transfer between models, or the role of data structure and low-variance directions.

questions.prompt: A vendor's product sheet says its traffic-sign recognizer is "robust to adversarial attacks and 97% accurate." You are asked to turn this claim into one that could be shown false. List what the claim must specify, explain why each item matters, and describe how you would report the evaluation so that a reader can see what was and was not tested.

rubric.text: Requires the set of allowed perturbations, such as the norm and size of the change, physical patches or transformations, and natural corruptions, because "robust" without a stated set has no input that would count as a failure.

Requires the attacker's knowledge and capability (white-box, query-only, transfer) and the attack's strength and adaptivity (steps, restarts, awareness of any defense), since weak attacks yield optimistic numbers and a measured robust accuracy is only an upper bound on worst-case accuracy.

Requires reporting clean accuracy and accuracy under each stated perturbation, with sample sizes or confidence intervals, and comparison with an undefended baseline, since robustness can be bought with clean accuracy.

Requires a separate axis for natural distribution shift (lighting, weather, camera changes, new regions), because robustness to constructed perturbations does not imply robustness to natural shift or the reverse.

Calls for a profile or table plus a residual-risk statement of perturbation types and shifts that were not tested, and notes that failing to find failures in a finite test is not proof of safety, so monitoring and a trigger for human review are needed.

questions.source: Adversarial training and its scaling limits
questions.prompt: Explain how adversarial training works, what it costs, and what it does not provide. Then say what else you would do before relying on an adversarially trained model in a safety-relevant application.

rubric.text: Describes the min–max structure: an inner maximization finds a high-loss perturbation inside the allowed set (for example by multi-step projected gradient ascent) and an outer minimization updates the weights to reduce the loss on those perturbed inputs.
States costs: roughly K + 1 forward-backward passes per batch for a K-step inner attack, and a typical loss of clean accuracy relative to ordinary training.
States that protection is tied to the threat model used in training (norm, budget, attack type) and transfers imperfectly to other norms, larger budgets, patches or natural shifts.

States that the resulting robustness is empirical, not a proof, since stronger or adaptive attacks may lower the measured accuracy, and mentions robust overfitting or the need to evaluate robust accuracy on held-out data and stop early.

Lists follow-up steps such as testing with strong adaptive attacks under several threat models, using certification or verification for narrow high-stakes properties, testing natural shift, monitoring in production, a human-review fallback and documenting residual risk.

questions.source: Certified defenses — what "guaranteed" means and costs
questions.prompt: Compare empirical robustness estimates (accuracy under the strongest attack you can run) with certified robustness (a proof that no perturbation in a stated set changes the prediction). For each, say what a reported number means, in which direction it can be wrong, and what its main limits are. Use randomized smoothing or a formal verifier as your example of a certificate. Recommend how to use them together.

rubric.text: Explains that accuracy under a given attack is an upper bound on true worst-case accuracy in that perturbation set, since failing to find an adversarial example does not prove none exists, and that weak, non-adaptive attacks or gradient masking inflate it.

Explains that certified accuracy counts only inputs for which a proof exists, so it is a lower bound on true robust accuracy, and that incomplete verifiers or loose certificates can understate robustness.

Notes that both statements hold only inside a stated perturbation set, such as an L2 radius or L∞ budget, and say nothing about other norms, larger budgets or natural shift, and that a certificate for one norm does not automatically cover another (an L2 radius R covers L∞ size ε only if ε√d ≤ R).

Names practical limits of certificates, such as many noise samples per prediction and a probabilistic guarantee for randomized smoothing, clean-accuracy loss at large noise levels, shrinking radii in high dimensions, and verification that scales poorly to large models or open-ended specifications.

Recommends reporting both, since certified ≤ true ≤ attack-measured brackets the truth, using stronger adaptive attacks to lower the upper bound and better methods to raise the lower bound, and reserving certification for narrow, high-stakes properties.

questions.prompt: A model that reads chest X-rays scores 94% on a held-out test set drawn from the same three hospitals used for training. The hospital is visible in image markers and is strongly correlated with disease prevalence. Explain how the model could score well for the wrong reason, how you would test whether it does, and what you would change in the data or the training if you find it does.

rubric.text: Explains shortcut learning: a feature that predicts the label in the training collection without being related to the disease (a hospital marker or scanner trait) is used by any model that minimizes training loss, and a random held-out split from the same sources has the same correlation, so it does not expose the shortcut.

Proposes baselines that use only the shortcut (the marker, or the image with the lung region masked) and compares them with 94%; if they come close, the score is weak evidence that the model reads pathology.
Proposes external evaluation on a new hospital and per-site or per-group results, including accuracy within each site-label combination, rather than one pooled figure.
Proposes intervention tests that add, remove or swap the marker while holding the image content fixed and check whether predictions move, noting that saliency maps alone are weak evidence.

Proposes remedies such as removing or randomizing markers, rebalancing or reweighting site-label groups, collecting data from more sites or group-robust training, and re-testing externally, while acknowledging that other site-specific cues may remain.

questions.prompt: Define covariate shift, label (prior) shift and concept shift. For each, give a concrete example, say how you would detect it in a deployed model, how you would evaluate or correct performance under it, and what could go wrong with your approach.

rubric.text: Defines all three correctly (P(x) changes with P(y | x) fixed; P(y) changes with P(x | y) fixed; P(y | x) changes) and gives a fitting example of each.

For covariate shift, describes detection by comparing input distributions (two-sample tests, a domain classifier, drift statistics), notes that detected shift may not hurt accuracy, and describes evaluation by importance weighting or by slicing performance over the shifted region, with the caveats of needing support overlap and of high-variance weights.

For label shift, describes estimating the new class frequencies from predicted-class counts and the confusion matrix or from a labeled sample, adjusting posteriors or thresholds by the prior ratio, and notes that true and false positive rates stay fixed while precision changes.

For concept shift, notes that it is invisible in inputs alone, so detection needs outcome labels or proxies, usually with a label delay, and that responses include retraining, recency weighting or windowing.

Gives caveats: real shifts mix types, which distribution is invariant cannot be verified from unlabeled data alone, drift monitors run many tests and need multiple-comparison control, and monitoring needs a trigger and an owner.

questions.prompt: A team iterates on a model for six months, checking the same 2000-example test set after every change (about 300 times), and then reports the final test accuracy as the accuracy to expect in production. Explain why that number is likely optimistic, describe two other ways an evaluation can leak, and describe an evaluation protocol that would give a trustworthy estimate.

rubric.text: Explains adaptive reuse and selection: choosing among many versions using the test set makes the final score partly a product of fitting that set's noise, so the test set has become a validation set and the estimate is biased upward, more so with more looks and a smaller test set.
Describes a leak through preprocessing or selection, such as normalization, imputation or feature selection fitted on all data (including labels) before the split.

Describes a second leak, such as duplicates or near-duplicates or the same entity on both sides of the split, temporal leakage from a random split of time-ordered data, features that encode the label, or benchmark contamination in pretraining data.

Describes a protocol with separate training, validation and untouched test sets, with the test set used once or a few times (or freshly collected), splits that match deployment (by time or by group), and preprocessing fitted inside training folds, with nested cross-validation when data are scarce.

Calls for reporting a confidence interval that reflects test size and disclosing how many comparisons were made, and notes that even a clean test estimates performance only on the sampling distribution, so deployment shift needs monitoring.

questions.prompt: A team runs 400 independent test cases, drawn at random from the expected usage of a system, and observes zero failures. Their report calls the failure rate "effectively zero". Evaluate this claim. Compute an approximate 95% upper confidence bound on the failure rate, say how many failure-free trials would be needed to bound the rate below 0.1%, and state the conditions under which the bound is valid and the ways it can mislead.

rubric.text: States that zero observed failures does not show a true rate of zero: the data are compatible with positive rates, for example a 1% rate would produce no failures in 400 trials with probability about 1.8%.
Gives the bound: by the rule of three, about 3/400 = 0.75% at 95% confidence (the exact value from (1 − p)^400 = 0.05 is about 0.746%).

Gives the requirement for 0.1%: about 3000 failure-free trials (n ≈ ln 0.05/ln 0.999 ≈ 2995), and notes that the bound shrinks in proportion to 1/n, so a tenfold smaller bound needs about ten times the trials.

States the conditions: independent draws from the distribution of interest, with clustered or near-duplicate cases reducing the effective sample size, and notes that the bound does not cover inputs outside the sampling distribution such as rare, shifted or adversarial inputs, or a test set reused after tuning.

Ties the bound to the decision: it should be compared with the tolerable failure rate, a ceiling of 0.75% may be unacceptable for severe events, and the report should state the bound and the sampling conditions rather than "zero".

questions.prompt: A support-ticket classifier reports about 93% overall accuracy. Broken down by customer segment, three large segments (together 95% of tickets) average 94.5% and one small segment (5% of tickets) scores 60%. Explain how the overall figure can hide this, what you would report and decide on, what could cause the pattern, and what limits any fix will face.

rubric.text: Shows that overall accuracy is a weighted average dominated by large groups: 0.95 × 94.5% + 0.05 × 60% ≈ 92.8%, so a segment at 60% barely moves it, and the overall figure would only fall to about 91% if that segment's share doubled to 10%.

Calls for reporting per-segment and worst-group accuracy with sample sizes and confidence intervals (small groups give wide intervals), and for basing the decision on consequences for the worst-affected group, not only the average.
Gives plausible causes, such as underrepresentation in training data, different label noise or a different input-label relationship in that segment, or reliance on cues that fail for it.

Gives mitigations such as collecting more data for the segment, reweighting or oversampling, group-robust objectives that minimize the worst group's loss, segment-specific thresholds or models, or human review for that segment.

States limits: group labels are needed at evaluation (and sometimes training), gains for one group may cost average accuracy, overlapping groups multiply and cannot all be enumerated, a small group's score can partly be noise, and improving known groups does not cover unknown ones.

questions.prompt: Distinguish robustness to natural perturbations (sensor noise, lighting changes, typos, a new population) from robustness to worst-case perturbations (inputs chosen by an optimizer within a budget). Explain why neither implies the other, give a high-dimensional argument for why random noise is a poor substitute for worst-case search, and design an evaluation plan for a deployed image classifier that covers both.

rubric.text: Defines natural perturbation as arising from the world or a shift in the data-generating process and worst-case perturbation as the loss-maximizing change inside a stated perturbation set, which makes the second depend on a threat model.

Explains that neither implies the other: an adversarially trained model can still degrade under natural shifts its training budget did not cover, and a model robust to noise or corruptions can be broken by small optimized changes.

Gives the high-dimensional argument: for a linear score the worst-case direction aligns with the weights and shifts the score by about ε‖w‖₁ (L∞) or r‖w‖₂ (L2), whereas a random direction of the same L2 length shifts it by about r‖w‖₂/√d, roughly √d times less.
Plans the natural axis: held-out data from other conditions or times, corruption tests, slice and worst-group metrics with confidence intervals, and monitoring of deployment inputs for drift.

Plans the worst-case axis: a stated threat model, strong adaptive multi-step attacks under several norms and budgets, black-box or transfer checks, and certification where feasible, reported as a profile with clean accuracy and residual risk.

questions.source: Cross-domain transfer — the same structure in different clothes
questions.prompt: You must test a toxicity classifier for a comment platform before launch, beyond its overall test accuracy. Design a stress-test suite that includes slice-based evaluation, invariance tests and counterfactual (minimal-pair) tests. For each, say what it would catch and what a pass does and does not establish, and explain how you would avoid fooling yourself given the number of tests you run.

rubric.text: Describes slice-based evaluation on predefined subsets (dialect, topic, length, language, identity terms, negation, quoted or reclaimed uses) with per-slice metrics, sample sizes and intervals, because averages hide pockets of failure.

Describes invariance tests that apply label-preserving edits (typos, case, whitespace, paraphrase, neutral name or identity-term swaps) and expect unchanged output, notes that failures expose dependence on surface cues, and notes that each edit must be checked to preserve the label.

Describes counterfactual or minimal-pair tests where a small edit should flip the label in a specified direction (adding negation, removing an insult), which reveals reliance on keywords rather than meaning.
States that passing a finite suite shows behavior only on those tests, that the tests encode their designers' assumptions, and that a pass does not prove invariance or understanding.

Describes statistical hygiene: many slices produce chance extremes, so slices should be predefined from a risk analysis, searched-for slices should be treated as hypotheses to confirm on fresh data, and the model should not be tuned on the stress suite and then evaluated on it as clean evidence.

questions.prompt: A company says its image classifier "understands" what a pedestrian is, citing 99% accuracy on a large test set. Without taking a position on what understanding is in general, describe what evidence about the classifier's behavior would be needed to support the narrower claim that it bases its decisions on the features that make something a pedestrian, explain why each kind of evidence is informative, and state what such evidence still could not establish.

rubric.text: Explains that high accuracy on a test set from the same source is consistent with reliance on accompanying cues (crosswalk, background, time of day) and cannot separate intended from incidental features.
Calls for stability under label-preserving changes (lighting, pose, clothing, background, small bounded perturbations), because a decision based on the intended features should not change with them.

Calls for sensitivity to meaningful interventions: predictions should change in the expected direction when a pedestrian is removed, added or occluded, tested with counterfactual edits that vary one factor at a time.
Calls for performance on shifted and rare conditions and on subgroups (other cities, sensors, weather, unusual poses) with worst-group results, not only an average.

States limits: finite tests give evidence about the conditions tested and not proof, behavior alone does not establish what is represented internally, saliency or other explanations are not proof of reliance, and humans must specify which features count as the right ones.

questions.source: Cross-domain transfer — the same structure in different clothes
questions.prompt: A lender deploys a default-prediction model on tabular applicant data, and applicants learn which fields move the score. Explain how adversarial robustness differs here from the image case, define a sensible threat model, and describe how you would change the model, the features and the evaluation to resist gaming.

rubric.text: Explains that tabular changes are discrete and bound by feasibility (debt cannot exceed what is possible, values must be non-negative, fields depend on one another), so unconstrained gradient attacks create impossible records and the real threat is strategic edits to feasible fields.
Classifies features as immutable, costly to change or cheap to change, and builds the threat model on what an applicant can change, at what cost and whether the lender verifies it.

Distinguishes features that cause repayment from proxies that merely correlate with it: cheap, non-causal proxies can be gamed so the score rises while risk does not, whereas causal features are costly to fake and improving them lowers real risk.
Proposes design changes such as favoring verified and causally relevant features, removing or down-weighting cheap proxies, monotonicity constraints, input verification and periodic retraining.

Proposes evaluation by searching over feasible costed edits and simulating best-response behavior, and notes that deployment itself changes the data (the relationship between features and default can drift), so monitoring and a retraining plan are required.

questions.source: Prompt sensitivity — the LLM-specific version of this problem
questions.prompt: A company uses a language model with a fixed instruction to label customer emails as urgent or not urgent. Design an evaluation of the labeler's robustness to wording and formatting changes, including how you would handle randomness in the outputs and how you would report results. Then explain how an adversarial email differs from a merely differently worded one.

rubric.text: Builds a set of meaning-preserving variants of the instruction and of the inputs (paraphrase, synonyms, formatting, whitespace, ordering, politeness), checked by reviewers to preserve the correct label.

Measures accuracy under each variant, the best-to-worst spread, and the share of items whose label stays the same across variants, with confidence intervals so that differences can be compared with sampling error.
Handles randomness: with stochastic decoding, repeats each condition several times to separate sampling variance from variance due to wording, or fixes the decoding settings and states them.
Reports the mean and worst case across variants rather than the best wording picked on the test data, with variants fixed in advance and any prompt tuning done on separate validation data.

Explains that an adversarial email is written or optimized to cause a wrong label or action (for example by embedding instructions to the model), which exploits the mixing of instructions and data, needs its own threat model and adaptive testing, and is not covered by passing paraphrase tests; mitigations include isolating untrusted text, limiting privileges and human review.

questions.source: The robustness toolkit — what each tool does and what it costs
questions.prompt: A paper reports a new defense for an image classifier with 88% accuracy under a one-step gradient-sign attack and 87% under a 10-step attack at the same L∞ budget, and claims state-of-the-art robustness. A reviewer notices that the defense includes random input transformations and a non-differentiable step, and finds that a black-box transfer attack from a surrogate model lowers accuracy to 35% at the same budget. Evaluate the claim: explain what the pattern of numbers suggests, which further experiments you would require, and what claim could responsibly be made.

rubric.text: Identifies the red flags: a black-box attack beating the white-box attacks, non-differentiable and random components, and almost no extra damage from ten steps, all pointing to gradient masking, so the high figures reflect attack failure and not insensitivity of the model.

Applies the upper-bound logic: accuracy under any real attack is an upper bound on worst-case accuracy, so the 35% result already shows worst-case accuracy at this budget is at most 35%, and the 88% claim is refuted under the paper's own threat model.

Requires adaptive attacks designed with knowledge of the defense (approximating the non-differentiable step with a differentiable one, averaging over the randomness), more steps and random restarts, and query-based black-box attacks.

Requires sanity checks and fuller reporting: accuracy should fall toward zero as the budget grows, results across several budgets and norms should be reported, and the minimum over all attacks with confidence intervals should be the headline.

States the claim that could be supported: robust accuracy at most the lowest value across attacks (35% so far), stated with the attack suite and residual risks, with any stronger claim requiring certification or verification.

questions.source: Adversarial training and its scaling limits
questions.prompt: A team can deploy either a standard classifier (95% clean accuracy, 0% accuracy under a worst-case perturbation of fixed budget) or an adversarially trained one (85% clean accuracy, 50% under the same attack). Defend a deployment choice for each of two settings: (a) a spam filter where some senders actively craft evasive messages, and (b) a photo-tagging feature in a personal app with no adversary. State what further information you would want.

rubric.text: States that the threat model decides which metric matters: in (a) adversaries probe and adapt, so worst-case accuracy is relevant, while in (b) there is no adversary, so clean accuracy and robustness to natural shift matter more.

Quantifies the trade: if a fraction f of inputs is attacked and the rest are clean, expected accuracy is 0.95(1 − f) for the standard model and 0.85(1 − f) + 0.5f for the robust one, which cross at f = 1/6 ≈ 17%, so the robust model wins when more than about one input in six is attacked at that budget.
Notes that neither number stands alone: the attack figure is an upper bound that depends on attack strength and budget realism, and the clean-accuracy cost may fall on particular slices.

Commits to a choice for each setting that follows from the stated threat model (typically the robust model or a layered defense for (a) and the standard model with natural-shift testing for (b)), and notes that in (a) adversaries adapt so static robustness decays, calling for retraining on new evasions, monitoring or human review.

Lists information to gather: realistic attacker budgets and share of adversarial traffic, relative costs of false positives and false negatives, per-slice and natural-shift accuracy, and compute and maintenance costs.

questions.source: What SHAP is, and what SHAP isn't
questions.prompt: A data scientist at a subscription company trains a gradient-boosted model to predict which customers will cancel within 90 days. A Shapley-value summary shows that "months since signup" has the largest average attribution, with longer tenure pushing the predicted cancellation probability down. The data scientist writes in a memo: "Tenure drives churn. If we give new customers a free six-month extension, they will stay." Evaluate this reasoning. Explain what the attribution does establish, why it does not support the proposed action, and what evidence would.

rubric.text: States that the attribution describes how the fitted model's prediction depends on the input relative to a reference, which is a fact about the model's behavior and not a causal effect in the world.

Explains that the model learned an association from observational data: long-tenured customers differ from new ones (survivors, plan type, satisfaction), so tenure can stand in for other causes of staying.

Notes that a free extension is an intervention on the customer's situation and is not the same variable as time elapsed since signup, so the model's dependence on tenure says nothing about what an extension would do.
Names the evidence that would support the action: a randomized experiment, or a credible causal design with confounders addressed, measuring cancellation and cost with and without the extension.
States what the attribution is good for here (generating hypotheses, checking the model's behavior for sense, spotting leakage) and concludes that the memo's claim remains a hypothesis until tested.

questions.source: Model Explainability: Distinguishing Explanation from the Appearance of Explanation
questions.prompt: A vendor claims that its saliency-map method for an image classifier "shows exactly what the model looks at", and offers as evidence that a panel of doctors found the maps reasonable. Design an evaluation that would test whether the maps are faithful to the model. For each test you propose, say what you would do, what result would count against the vendor's claim, and what the test cannot show. Also explain why the doctors' ratings do not answer the question.

rubric.text: Distinguishes plausibility (judged by people) from faithfulness (reflecting what the model computes), and explains that doctors' ratings test the former: a faithful map of a model that uses a spurious cue can look wrong, and an unfaithful map can look right.
Proposes replacing the trained weights with random ones (fully or layer by layer) and checking that the maps change substantially; maps that stay similar do not depend on what the model learned.
Proposes training on shuffled labels, or a similar data randomization, and comparing the resulting maps with those of the real model.

Proposes a deletion or insertion test, removing or revealing the top-ranked regions and comparing the change in the model's output with the change from random regions, while noting that masked images are off-distribution.

States the limits: passing these tests is necessary but not sufficient, none shows causal relevance in the real world, and the method should be compared with alternatives and checked on planted cues whose ground truth is known.

questions.prompt: A hospital's readmission model is additive: predicted risk (%) = 4 + 0.3 x age + 2.5 x prior admissions - 1.5 x follow-up visits in the last year. A patient aged 80 with 3 prior admissions and 0 follow-up visits has a predicted risk of 35.5%. Explain this prediction with Shapley values, treating the inputs as independent and valuing a subset of inputs as the expected prediction when those inputs are fixed at the patient's values and the others are set to a reference group's averages. Use two reference groups. Group 1 is all adult patients, averaging age 55, 1 prior admission and 2 follow-up visits. Group 2 is patients aged 75 to 85, averaging age 80, 2 prior admissions and 1 follow-up visit. Compute the three Shapley values for each reference group and check them against the model's predictions. Explain why age is the top reason against one reference and not the other, and say which reference you would use and how you would present the result to a clinician.

rubric.text: Shows that in an additive model with independent inputs each Shapley value equals the coefficient times the patient's deviation from the reference average.
Against group 1 gives age +7.5, prior admissions +5.0 and follow-up visits +3.0, summing to +15.5, the gap between 35.5% and the group's average prediction of 20.0%.
Against group 2 gives age 0, prior admissions +2.5 and follow-up visits +1.5, summing to +4.0, the gap between 35.5% and the group's average prediction of 31.5%.

Explains that an attribution answers "compared with what?": against all adults age is the main reason because the patient is older, against peers of the same age it explains nothing, and the model has not changed.
Recommends choosing the reference that matches the clinical question, stating it with every explanation, and checking how the conclusion changes under other references.

questions.prompt: Two teams train models for the same lending task on the same data. Team 1 uses a gradient-boosted tree model and team 2 a regularized logistic regression. Both reach a test AUC of 0.86 (the difference is within sampling noise) and the two models make the same decision for 94% of applicants. Team 1's Shapley-based ranking puts total_debt first; team 2's ranking puts monthly_payments first. The two inputs have a correlation of 0.9. A manager asks which ranking identifies "the true driver" of lending outcomes and wants to publish one. Explain why both rankings can be accurate descriptions of their models while neither identifies a true driver, what you would do to produce a more defensible statement about importance, and what the report should say.

rubric.text: Explains that many different models can fit the data about equally well, so predictive accuracy does not select among them, and that an attribution is a property of one fitted model.

Explains that with strongly correlated inputs a model can substitute one for the other, so credit shifts between them according to the algorithm, the regularization and the random seed rather than the world.
Says that neither ranking establishes a causal driver of repayment; that takes causal knowledge or an experiment.

Proposes concrete checks: repeating across seeds, bootstrap resamples and several model classes, and attributing to the group of correlated inputs together (for example by permuting them jointly), then comparing the results.
Says what to report: that the ranking is not unique, which model each ranking describes, how stable it was, and the group-level finding, rather than a single "true driver".

questions.source: Counterfactuals are closer to what you actually want
questions.prompt: A lender must tell denied applicants what they could do to be approved. A data scientist proposes to return, for each denied applicant, the closest approved input found by an optimizer (Euclidean distance on standardized features) and to tell the applicant to change to those values. Critique this proposal. Identify at least four distinct ways the returned counterfactual can be useless or harmful as advice, and propose a design change for each.

rubric.text: Notes that the search can change immutable or sensitive inputs (age, sex, past events) or move one-way inputs (a past missed payment cannot be removed, tenure only grows with time), so constraints on what may change must be built in; a result that needs an immutable input also signals that the model relies on it.
Notes that distance in standardized units is not the applicant's cost or effort, and proposes a cost function reflecting effort and time and offering several diverse options.

Notes that inputs are correlated or causally linked, so a point reached by changing a few inputs while holding the rest fixed may not be reachable, and proposes plausibility or causal-consistency constraints.
Notes that the counterfactual describes the current model and threshold, which can change with retraining or policy, and proposes stating a validity period and re-checking or committing to it.

Notes that flipping the model's output is not evidence that the applicant would repay and that advice can encourage gaming of proxies, and proposes tracking the outcomes of applicants who follow the advice.

questions.source: Model Explainability: Distinguishing Explanation from the Appearance of Explanation
questions.prompt: A team's skin-lesion classifier scores AUC 0.95 in internal validation but 0.78 at a new clinic. Attribution maps on internal images concentrate on a ruler and on ink marks that clinicians often add near lesions they find suspicious. Describe how you would use explanations to investigate, how you would confirm a suspected shortcut with methods that do not rely on the explanation, and how you would fix the problem and verify the fix.

rubric.text: Uses attributions across many images, not one, to form a hypothesis about which regions or features carry weight, split by correct and incorrect cases and by class.

Confirms by an intervention that does not rely on the explanation: removing or inpainting the markers, adding them to benign images, and measuring how predictions and accuracy change, and comparing accuracy on images with and without markers.

Checks provenance: how marker presence relates to the label in the training data (marked cases were more often suspicious or biopsied) and how that differs at the new clinic, stratifying by site and device.

Proposes fixes such as removing or masking the cue, rebalancing or collecting data where the cue is uncorrelated with the label, augmentation, or training that penalizes reliance on it, followed by retraining.
Verifies on an external site and on cue-swapped test sets, re-inspects the attributions, and notes that an explanation is a lead rather than proof because other shortcuts may remain.

questions.source: Model Explainability: Distinguishing Explanation from the Appearance of Explanation
questions.prompt: A company deploys a language model that writes step-by-step reasoning before answering in a medical-coding task, and plans to show that reasoning to auditors as the explanation of why each code was chosen. Evaluate whether the written reasoning can serve as an explanation of the model's decision. Describe an experiment that tests it, and say what the auditors can and cannot conclude from the text.

rubric.text: Distinguishes a rationale that reads plausibly from a faithful account of the factors that produced the output, noting that the reasoning is itself generated text and not a readout of the model's computation.
Describes an intervention experiment: change or add a factor in the input (for example a hint or an irrelevant cue), see whether the answer changes, and see whether the reasoning mentions the factor.
Describes a second test, such as corrupting or removing steps of the reasoning and checking whether the answer changes, or checking whether the answer is stable when the reasoning is regenerated.

States what auditors can use the reasoning for (finding errors, checking cited rules against sources, making steps reviewable) and what they cannot conclude (that it lists all influences or shows the absence of bias).
Recommends verifying the claims in the reasoning against source documents and outcome data, and not treating the text as evidence of what caused the decision.

questions.source: Three words that don't mean the same thing
questions.prompt: A city agency will use a model to prioritize housing-inspection visits, and the decisions affect landlords and tenants. A vendor offers (a) a gradient-boosted model with AUC 0.88 and post-hoc Shapley explanations, and (b) a scoring rule with seven integer-weighted checks and AUC 0.86. Argue for the option you would adopt and the evidence you would demand before deciding. Address the accuracy gap, the reliability of the explanations, auditability, and what would change your decision.

rubric.text: Asks whether the 0.02 AUC gap is real and matters: compares the options on the same held-out data with uncertainty (for example bootstrap intervals) and on an operational metric such as violations found in the top-k visits, not AUC alone.

Notes that for the scoring rule the model is its own exact explanation, so reviewers, tenants and landlords can check, contest and correct it, whereas a post-hoc explanation describes a model that remains opaque and can be approximate, unstable or misleading with correlated inputs.
Notes that neither option's explanations show that decisions are fair or correct, so both need outcome audits across neighborhoods and groups and monitoring for drift.
Gives the case for the complex model if its operational advantage is large and important, with conditions such as validation, monitoring, and keeping the simple rule as a benchmark or fallback.

States what would change the decision: a larger operational gap, evidence that the simple rule fails in subgroups, legal requirements for reasons, or the results of a stability analysis of the explanations.

questions.prompt: A manager runs LIME, which explains a prediction by fitting a simple model to the classifier's outputs on randomly perturbed copies of the input, twice on the same input of a deterministic classifier and gets different top features. She asks: "Which explanation is correct?" Answer her question. Explain what the output actually is, what causes the variation, and the procedure you would follow to give her a reliable characterization of the classifier's local behavior on this input.

rubric.text: Says neither run is "the" correct explanation: each is one random estimate from a fit to randomly sampled perturbed points, so the question assumes a single true answer that the method does not return.

Names sources of variation: random sampling of perturbed points, the number of samples, the neighborhood width or kernel, feature discretization, and regularization of the surrogate, while the classifier itself is deterministic.
Describes repeating the run with many seeds and more samples until it is stable, quantifying agreement (for example top-k overlap or rank correlation), and reporting coefficients with their spread.
Describes checking the surrogate's local fidelity (weighted R-squared on the neighborhood), its sensitivity to the neighborhood width, and whether the perturbed points are realistic.
Describes checking the explanation against the classifier by applying the suggested changes to the real model and comparing outputs, and cautions against picking the run that looks most sensible.

questions.source: What SHAP is, and what SHAP isn't
questions.prompt: A team must give a regulator a feature-importance report for a random-forest model of loan default. Three tools are available: the forest's built-in impurity-based importance, permutation importance on held-out data, and the mean absolute Shapley value over the held-out set. Compare what each measures, name a failure mode of each, and propose a protocol that makes the report defensible. State what the report can and cannot claim.

rubric.text: Describes impurity-based importance as the total impurity reduction from splits on training data, and names its failure modes: it can reward fitting noise, it favors inputs with many distinct values, and it says nothing about generalization.

Describes permutation importance as the drop in held-out performance when a column is shuffled (the model's reliance), and notes that correlated inputs distort it through unrealistic shuffled rows and shared credit, which permuting correlated groups together mitigates.

Describes mean absolute Shapley value as the average size of an input's contribution to predictions relative to a reference, noting that it depends on the reference and value function, measures influence on outputs rather than on accuracy, and splits credit among correlated inputs.

Proposes a protocol: held-out data, repeated runs or bootstrap for variability, a random noise column as a null benchmark, grouping of correlated inputs, reporting more than one measure with their disagreements, and documenting the model, reference and settings.
States the limits: all three describe the fitted model's dependence and not causal importance in the world, so claims about real-world drivers need causal evidence.

questions.source: Three words that don't mean the same thing
questions.prompt: A proposed rule would require that any automated decision denying someone a benefit be accompanied by "a clear explanation of the main factors". A vendor proposes to satisfy it by printing the three inputs with the largest Shapley values for each decision. Evaluate whether this serves the purposes such a rule would have: understanding the decision, contesting it and correcting errors, acting to change the outcome, and detecting discrimination. For each purpose say what the list does or does not supply and what would need to be added.

rubric.text: For understanding: notes that attributions are relative to a reference and depend on the model, so the person needs plain-language statements of the main factors with the values used, and that adequacy depends on the audience.

For contesting and correcting: notes that showing which recorded values drove the decision lets a person spot a wrong input and request correction, but does not show whether the model's logic is sound.

For acting to change the outcome: notes that a list of contributions is not recourse, and that the person also needs counterfactual information restricted to changes they can make and the size of change needed.
For detecting discrimination: notes that per-decision top-three lists cannot reveal proxy effects or group disparities, which need outcome audits by group and tests with matched cases.
Notes that the list may be approximate or unstable, can omit interactions and correlated inputs, and recommends adding counterfactuals, documentation of the method and a route to human review.

questions.prompt: A model's expected output given each subset of three inputs is: no inputs, 50; A alone, 60; B alone, 55; C alone, 50; A and B, 75; A and C, 60; B and C, 55; all three, 75. (a) Compute the Shapley values of A, B and C. (b) Check them against the total to be explained. (c) Explain what the result shows about C and about the interaction between A and B. (d) Explain why one-at-a-time effects (the change from adding each input alone to the empty set) would give a misleading picture here.

rubric.text: Gives the Shapley values A = 15, B = 10 and C = 0, with a method: the average of marginal contributions over the six orderings, or the coalition weights 1/3, 1/6, 1/6 and 1/3.
Checks that 15 + 10 + 0 = 25 = 75 - 50, the output with all inputs minus the output with none (efficiency).
Explains that C never changes the output in any coalition, so it is a dummy input and receives 0.
Explains that A and B together add 10 beyond their separate effects (10 and 5, against a joint gain of 25) and that the Shapley value splits that synergy equally, 5 to each.

Explains that the one-at-a-time effects (10, 5 and 0) sum to 15 and miss the synergy, and that an attribution based on a single ordering would give A and B different shares depending on which is added first.

questions.source: Model Explainability: Distinguishing Explanation from the Appearance of Explanation
questions.prompt: A hospital wants to know whether showing feature-attribution explanations next to an AI risk score helps clinicians decide better. Design the study. Specify the arms, the outcome measures, which results you would analyze separately, how you would handle sample size and uncertainty, and what results would lead you not to deploy the explanations.

rubric.text: Specifies randomized arms: at least the AI score alone and the AI score with the explanation, preferably with a no-AI control, with random assignment and an analysis plan fixed in advance.
Includes cases on which the AI is right and cases on which it is wrong, and reports decision accuracy separately for each so that overreliance on wrong advice is visible.
Measures reliance and calibration, for example agreement with the AI, changes of mind, clinician confidence compared with accuracy, and time taken.

Handles the statistics: justifies the sample size for the effect of interest, reports confidence intervals for differences in proportions, accounts for clustering by clinician and case, and does not read a non-significant result as no effect.

States decision criteria in advance: do not deploy if explanations raise following of wrong advice or fail to improve accuracy beyond the score alone, since confidence without accuracy is unwarranted trust.

questions.prompt: An auditor receives from a lender a set of Shapley and LIME reports for 1,000 loan decisions. The reports were generated by the lender, show zero importance for a sensitive attribute, and have consistent top features. The lender offers them as proof that its model does not use the attribute. Explain how this evidence could mislead, including by deliberate design, and describe what the auditor should do instead.

rubric.text: Notes that the reports were generated, and possibly selected, by the party being audited, with its own reference and settings, and cannot be tied to the deployed model without access.
Notes that perturbation-based explainers query unrealistic points and that a deployed system can be built to behave differently on them, so the reports can be made to look clean.
Notes that zero attribution to an attribute (for example because it is excluded from the inputs) does not rule out dependence through correlated proxies.
Proposes testing the deployed system directly: matched pairs of realistic applications that differ in the attribute or its proxies, and outcome and error rates by group on real decisions.
Proposes independent replication with the auditor's own explainers and settings, access to the model and its logs, and comparison of the explanations with measured behavior.

questions.prompt: A colleague argues: "SHAP, which assigns each input its Shapley value, is the only attribution method that satisfies efficiency (attributions sum to the prediction minus a baseline prediction), symmetry (interchangeable inputs get equal values), dummy (an input that never matters gets zero) and additivity (attributions for a sum of two models are the sums of their attributions), so it is the uniquely correct way to explain a model's predictions." Evaluate the argument. Say where it is valid, where it overreaches, and what the word "correct" hides.

rubric.text: States the valid core: for a given value function (a rule assigning a payoff to each subset of inputs), the Shapley allocation is the unique one satisfying the four properties.

Points out that the uniqueness is conditional on the value function: marginal versus conditional sampling and the choice of reference distribution give different attributions for the same model, and the axioms do not choose among them.
Points out that the properties describe a fair split of a total and do not guarantee that the split answers the user's question, such as causal effect, recourse or which inputs to collect.

Gives examples where all four properties hold and the output still misleads: credit split between duplicate inputs, interaction credit divided equally, attributions that do not predict the effect of changing an input, and approximations used when exact computation is infeasible.

Concludes that "uniquely correct" overreaches: the accurate claim is that it uniquely satisfies these properties for a stated value function, and that usefulness must be judged against the purpose and audience.

questions.source: Three flavors of bias, mapped to the ten types
questions.prompt: A company wants to build a model that ranks job applicants for interview, trained on its own hiring and performance records from the past ten years. Take five different stages of the machine-learning pipeline, from the world that produced the data to the way the ranking is used. For each stage give one concrete way a disparity between groups could enter and one check that could detect it.

rubric.text: Covers the world and history: past hiring and promotion decisions reflect earlier practices, so labels recording who was hired can encode earlier disparities even when the records are accurate; a check compares the label with an independent outcome measure or examines variation across decision-makers.

Covers sampling and representation: who appears in the data (applicants screened out earlier have no performance outcomes, and some groups may be thinly represented); a check compares the composition of the data with the population the model will be applied to.

Covers measurement, labels and features: proxies for group (postcode, school, gaps in employment) or measurement that is noisier or more biased for some groups; a check predicts group from the features or ablates a suspect feature and watches the gap.

Covers model, objective and evaluation: training on average loss favours the largest group and pooled metrics hide weak subgroups; a check reports disaggregated metrics with uncertainty, including intersectional groups.

Covers deployment and use: how cutoffs and human reviewers act on the ranking and the feedback loop in which people hired under the model generate the next training data; a check tracks outcome rates by group at each decision stage after deployment.

questions.source: Leverage analysis — finding the high-leverage intervention point
questions.prompt: A bank removes the field "gender" from the inputs of its credit-scoring model and announces: "The model never sees gender, so it cannot discriminate by gender." Evaluate this claim. Explain what could still go wrong, how you would test for it, and what the bank should do in addition.

rubric.text: Explains that other inputs correlated with gender (occupation, spending categories, part-time work history) let a model reconstruct much of the removed information, so outcomes can still differ by gender.
Explains that a model learns whatever predicts its training labels, so if the labels reflect past disparities by gender the model can reproduce them through correlated inputs.

Describes a test for proxies, such as trying to predict gender from the remaining inputs (high accuracy means the information is present) and comparing outcomes by gender or re-scoring with suspect inputs removed.

Notes that correlation with gender does not by itself show improper use, because a correlated input may carry legitimate information about repayment, so inputs should be judged by their effects and by the cost of dropping them.

Notes that deleting the attribute also removes the ability to measure outcomes by group, so the field should be retained for auditing where the law allows, and that mitigation at other stages should be considered.

questions.prompt: A hospital audit finds that a triage model refers 24% of patients from group X (1,200 of 5,000) to a specialist programme and 15% of patients from group Y (450 of 3,000), a ratio of 1.6, and the difference is far too large to be chance. A manager concludes: "The model is biased against group Y." Explain why the gap alone does not establish this, and design an investigation that would separate the possible causes. For each test, say what it can and cannot show.

rubric.text: States that the gap is a descriptive measurement consistent with several causes, such as differences in clinical need, in how the data were collected, in labels, in the model, in cutoffs or in downstream review, and that its size or significance does not say which.

Proposes stratifying or adjusting for clinically legitimate variables (severity, diagnosis) to see whether the gap persists among comparable patients, and notes the limits: unmeasured factors, and adjustment variables that may themselves be shaped by group.

Proposes a matched or counterfactual comparison, such as scoring paired records that differ only in group-related inputs, and notes that it shows whether the model's output depends on those inputs but not why the populations differ, and that group often cannot be changed alone.
Proposes ablating or substituting one pipeline stage at a time (labels, individual features, the cutoff, the human review step) and tracking how the gap changes, to locate where it arises.
Reports uncertainty and alternatives: confidence intervals, a plan for subgroups, and the point that results narrow the hypotheses rather than prove a cause, with the remaining explanations stated.

questions.prompt: A lender reports approval counts for two groups across two loan products. Secured loans: group P has 70 approvals out of 100 applications and group Q has 300 out of 500. Unsecured loans: group P has 150 out of 500 and group Q has 20 out of 100. An analyst says the aggregate figures show group P is treated worse than group Q. Compute the rates, explain how the comparison can reverse once the product is considered, say which comparison should be reported and what further information you would need to decide, and state what you can and cannot conclude.

rubric.text: Computes the rates: group P is approved for 70% of secured and 30% of unsecured applications (220 of 600, about 36.7%, overall) and group Q for 60% and 20% (320 of 600, about 53.3%, overall), so P is ahead within each product but behind overall.

Explains the arithmetic: each overall rate is an average of the product rates weighted by that group's application mix, and group P applies mostly for the low-approval unsecured product while group Q applies mostly for the secured one.
Describes a standardized comparison on a common product mix (for example a 50/50 mix gives 50% for P and 40% for Q) as a way to compare the groups on equal footing.

States that neither table is automatically correct: if product choice is independent of the lender's process the within-product comparison is fairer, but if the lender steers groups into products the overall gap may reflect real disadvantage that stratifying hides.

Names the information needed (why applicants chose different products, applicant risk within products, who set the mix) and concludes that the data alone support a description and a conditional claim, not a verdict on bias.

questions.prompt: A team reports that its classifier is 96.5% accurate on a 12,000-example test set. A subgroup of 300 test examples has 36 errors (a 12% error rate, with a 95% interval of about 8.8% to 16.2%), against about 3.3% error on the other 11,700 examples. The subgroup can be split further by a second attribute into four cells of roughly 75 examples each. Explain what the headline number hides and design an evaluation that reports performance by subgroup responsibly, including how to treat the small cells.

rubric.text: Explains that overall accuracy is a size-weighted average dominated by the large group, so a subgroup with a much higher error rate (12% against 3.3%) can sit behind an excellent headline figure.
Requires disaggregated metrics, including the error types that matter (false positives and false negatives), reported for each subgroup rather than only pooled.

Requires uncertainty on every subgroup figure and explains that cells of about 75 examples give wide intervals (a 12% error rate on 75 examples is roughly 6% to 21%), so a non-significant difference does not show parity.

Addresses intersections and multiplicity: crossing attributes multiplies the number of cells, small cells need more data or deliberate oversampling for the audit, and subgroups should be chosen before looking at results or corrected for multiple comparisons to limit chance findings.
Says the test data should resemble the deployment population and that the report should state what cannot be concluded from cells that remain too small.

questions.prompt: A firm trains a model to predict who will be promoted, using ten years of its own promotion records, and finds the model is highly accurate on held-out records. In those years promotions went to one group at a higher rate than to others with comparable measured performance. Argue whether the model's accuracy is evidence that it is fair, explain why standard data-quality checks may find nothing wrong, and describe what the firm could do about the label.

rubric.text: Explains that the label records what decision-makers did, not what ought to have happened, so a model that predicts it well reproduces past patterns and its accuracy measures fidelity to the past rather than fairness.
Explains that the records can be complete, correctly entered and representative and still carry the disparity, so data-quality and sampling checks do not detect it.
Describes a diagnostic: compare promotion rates by group among employees with similar independently measured performance, and look at variation across decision-makers or periods.

Describes options with their limits (a less biased outcome measure, down-weighting earlier periods, constraints that reduce reliance on group-correlated signals), each trading fit to the past against fairness, and says how much to trade is a value judgement.
Notes that an alternative outcome measure has its own distortions, that deployment should be monitored, and that it may be right not to automate the decision when no defensible target exists.

questions.prompt: A lender approves loans only for applicants whose score exceeds a cutoff, and it learns whether a borrower defaults only if the loan was granted. The lender wants to retrain its model and to estimate how many creditworthy applicants it has been turning away. Explain why the observed data are a problem, what goes wrong if the lender trains and evaluates on approved applicants only, and describe at least two ways of addressing the problem together with the limits of each.

rubric.text: Defines the problem: outcomes are observed only for applicants who received the favourable decision, and the earlier policy made that decision, so the labelled data are a selected subset rather than a random one.

Explains the consequences: performance measured on approved applicants does not describe performance on rejected ones, and error rates for rejected applicants, such as how many would have repaid, cannot be computed from the data at all.

Describes randomized exploration (approving a small random sample of applicants below the cutoff) as producing unbiased outcomes for the rejected region, and notes its cost and ethical considerations.

Describes a second approach such as reject inference, bounds or sensitivity analysis, or using natural variation in decision-makers' leniency, and states that these rely on assumptions (for example no unmeasured confounding) that cannot be verified from the data.
Says findings should be reported with the uncertainty that comes from the unobserved region, and that the old policy's bias carries into any model trained naively on the approved applicants.

questions.source: Leverage analysis — finding the high-leverage intervention point
questions.prompt: A city uses a system that sends inspectors to the neighbourhoods with the most violations recorded last quarter. Two neighbourhoods have the same true violation rate, but one starts with more recorded violations. Explain how the system's decisions affect its own future data, what happens to the two neighbourhoods' records over time, why collecting more data does not correct this, and how the city could detect and break the loop.

rubric.text: Explains the mechanism: violations are recorded where inspectors look, so the number recorded depends on inspection effort as well as on the true rate, and sending inspectors by past records makes new records reflect past allocation.

Explains the outcome: the initial imbalance is self-confirming, equal true rates still produce records that show the heavily inspected area as worse, and an allocation rule that rewards the leader more than proportionally makes the gap grow.
Explains that more data from the same process cannot correct it, because every new record is shaped by the allocation, so the estimate stays biased even as it becomes more precise.

Describes detection: compare the records with a measurement independent of inspector presence (complaints, surveys, random inspections) and check whether recorded rates track effort, for example by looking at rates per inspection hour.
Describes ways to break the loop: randomized or exploratory allocation of some effort, normalizing counts by effort, limits on how far allocation follows past records, and periodic audits.

questions.source: Leverage analysis — finding the high-leverage intervention point
questions.prompt: A screening model selects 40% of applicants from group A and 20% from group B. The team wants to narrow this gap. Describe how a pre-processing, an in-processing and a post-processing approach would each work, the main limitation of each, and the circumstances in which none of the three would address the real problem.

rubric.text: Describes a pre-processing approach (reweighing or resampling the training examples, relabelling, or removing or transforming features) and its limitation: it changes the data the model sees but does not guarantee fair predictions or correct inaccurate labels for individuals.

Describes an in-processing approach (a fairness penalty or constraint in the training objective, or adversarial training) and its limitation: it needs group information during training, gives up some agreement with the training labels, and satisfies only the chosen criterion.

Describes a post-processing approach (group-specific cutoffs or adjusted scores) and its limitation: it works with any trained model but treats applicants with the same score differently by group, needs group at decision time, and leaves the learned scores unchanged.

Identifies when none work: when the disparity comes from a biased label, from measurement of differing quality across groups, or from the downstream process (reviewers, cutoffs, feedback), because these methods operate on the model's fit to the labels and the metrics.
States that the choice should follow a diagnosis of where the gap arises, that the effect must be checked on held-out data with uncertainty, and that improving one metric can worsen others.

questions.source: A limit case: when the leverage is upstream of your pipeline — and who owns it then
questions.prompt: A hospital system deploys a risk-prediction product built by a vendor, trained on a dataset assembled by a third party and labelled by clinicians at another institution. After deployment, patients from one group are found to be flagged less often at the same level of illness. Explain how responsibility should be mapped across the parties, what documentation would make that mapping inspectable (and what each document should contain), and what role an independent audit plays.

rubric.text: Maps decisions to the parties who control them (data collection, labelling, model training, the cutoff and use in care, monitoring) and explains that accountability follows control, with the deploying hospital remaining accountable for its use of the tool.
Describes a datasheet for the dataset: how and why the data were collected, who is and is not represented, how and by whom labels were produced, known gaps and recommended uses.
Describes a model card for the model: intended and out-of-scope uses, the evaluation data, performance broken down by subgroup with uncertainty, and known limitations.

Describes an independent audit: the auditor can access or query the model and data, reproduces the reported numbers, tests subgroups the developer did not choose, and records the model version evaluated.

States the limits: documents are disclosures that can be incomplete or out of date, they do not make a system fair, and they must be kept current and used in procurement and monitoring decisions for responsibility to be inspectable.

questions.prompt: A classifier has a true positive rate of 75% and a false positive rate of 10% in each of two groups. The base rate (the share who are truly positive) is 20% in group 1 and 40% in group 2. Compute the positive predictive value (the share of flagged people who are truly positive) in each group. Then explain what this shows about trying to equalize error rates and positive predictive value at the same time, state the conditions under which the conflict disappears, and say who should decide how to resolve it.

rubric.text: Computes a positive predictive value of about 65.2% for group 1 and about 83.3% for group 2 (0.15 / 0.23 and 0.30 / 0.36).
Explains the mechanism: PPV depends on the base rate as well as on the error rates, PPV = p x TPR / (p x TPR + (1 - p) x FPR), so equal TPR and FPR with different base rates give different PPV.
Shows that equalizing PPV would require different error rates (for example, keeping TPR at 75%, group 2's FPR would have to rise to about 26.7%), so the criteria cannot all hold together.
States the assumptions: the conflict arises when base rates differ and the classifier is imperfect, and it disappears when base rates are equal or the classifier is perfect.

Says the choice among criteria is a values decision about which errors are more costly and who bears them, to be made and documented by accountable parties with affected people consulted, and notes that unequal base rates may themselves reflect measurement or historical distortions worth examining.
